first-pandyan-empire.t: The revived Pandya kingdom of Madurai, which drove out the Kalabhras and dominated the far south for three centuries.
first-pandyan-empire.o: Around 590 the [[e:pandya-dynasty|Pandya]] king Kadungon overthrew the [[s:kalabhra-dynasty|Kalabhra dynasty]] in the [[e:madurai|Madurai]] region, reviving the line of the [[s:early-pandyas|Early Pandyas]]. His successors expanded into the Kaveri delta and the Kongu country, competing with the [[s:pallava-dynasty|Pallava dynasty]] and the [[s:chalukyas-of-badami|Chalukyas of Badami]].
first-pandyan-empire.r: Arikesari Maravarman, according to Shaiva tradition, was converted from Jainism by the saint Sambandar, and the Bhakti movement of the Nayanars and Alvars flourished under [[e:pandya-dynasty|Pandya]] patronage. The Velvikudi [[e:copper|copper]] plates of Jatila Parantaka Nedunjadaiyan trace the dynasty's history in [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and Tamil. Pandya kings issued land grants, built rock-cut temples and controlled the pearl fisheries. Srimara Srivallabha invaded [[s:sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]] and sacked Anuradhapura in the 9th century.
first-pandyan-empire.e: Varaguna II was defeated at Sripurambiyam around 885 by the [[s:pallava-dynasty|Pallavas]] and their allies. Around 920 Parantaka I of the [[s:chola-empire|Chola Empire]] defeated Rajasimha III, who fled to [[s:sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]]. The [[s:later-pandyan-empire|Pandyas]] survived as [[e:chola-empire|Chola]] [[e:vassal|vassals]] and later revived again in the 13th century.

free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.t: An Alsatian wine town beneath a Hohenstaufen castle that was a free imperial city and Decapolis member until French annexation.
free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.o: The castle of Kaysersberg was built in the 1220s for [[e:frederick-ii|Frederick II]] to guard the route from Alsace into [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Lorraine]] over the Vosges, and a town grew at its foot. It received imperial-city privileges in 1293 and in 1354 joined the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], the defensive league of ten Alsatian imperial cities under the emperor's bailiff at [[s:free-imperial-city-of-haguenau|Haguenau]].
free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.r: Ruled by a council and mayor, Kaysersberg was a modest community of vintners, craftsmen and traders whose wealth came from the wine of the surrounding slopes. The preacher Johann Geiler of Kaysersberg, the most famous pulpit voice of late medieval [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]], grew up there and took his name from the town, which remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg.e: Like the other [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]] cities it came under French protection after 1648, and the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679 completed its incorporation into the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]]. Albert Schweitzer was born there in 1875. It is now a small town in the Haut-Rhin [[e:departement|department]].

free-imperial-city-of-reutlingen.t: Swabian imperial city below the Jura that beat the Count of Württemberg in 1377 and was one of two cities to sign the Augsburg Confession in 1530.
free-imperial-city-of-reutlingen.o: Reutlingen grew at the foot of the Achalm hill on the edge of the Swabian Jura, and was fortified and granted town rights by the Hohenstaufen around 1240, becoming an imperial city. Its walls soon had to resist the counts of Württemberg, whose territory surrounded it.
free-imperial-city-of-reutlingen.r: [[e:guild|Guilds]] came to dominate the council, an unusual feature among Swabian cities. In 1377 the townsmen defeated Ulrich of Württemberg at the Battle of Reutlingen, a high point of the Swabian city leagues. Cloth and leather were its main trades. Under the preacher Matthäus Alber it adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 1520s, and in 1530 it was one of only two cities to sign the [[s:free-imperial-city-of-augsburg|Augsburg]] Confession, with [[s:free-imperial-city-of-nuremberg|Nuremberg]].
free-imperial-city-of-reutlingen.e: A great fire in 1726 destroyed much of the town. Reutlingen lost its freedom in 1802, when it was annexed by Württemberg, and it is now a city in Baden-Württemberg; the Gothic Marienkirche survived the fire.

free-imperial-city-of-zell-am-harmersbac.t: One of the smallest free imperial cities, a Black Forest town in the Harmersbach valley that kept its independence until 1803.
free-imperial-city-of-zell-am-harmersbac.o: Zell grew in the Harmersbach valley near the abbey of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-gengenbach|Gengenbach]] and was recognised as a free imperial city in the 14th century, with its status confirmed in 1366. With the Free Imperial City of Gengenbach and [[s:free-imperial-city-of-offenburg|Offenburg]] it lay within the Ortenau bailiwick, which emperors often pledged to neighbouring lords.
free-imperial-city-of-zell-am-harmersbac.r: With only a few hundred inhabitants, Zell was among the tiniest imperial estates, governed by a council and mayor. The town and the neighbouring free valley of Harmersbach, an unusual imperial community of peasants, lived from forestry, farming and crafts. Zell remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-zell-am-harmersbac.e: The mediatisation of 1803 gave Zell to Baden. Its pottery works, founded in 1794 and later known as Zeller Keramik, made the town's name in the 19th century. It is now a small town in Baden-Württemberg.

fort-dauphin-colony.t: France's first colony on Madagascar, a struggling trading post on the south-east coast that ended in massacre and evacuation in 1674.
fort-dauphin-colony.o: In 1643 the French Company of the East (Compagnie de l'Orient) sent Jacques Pronis to establish a post in south-east Madagascar. He founded Fort-Dauphin, named after the future [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]], in the lands of the [[s:antanosy-kingdom|Antanosy Kingdom]] near modern Taolagnaro.
fort-dauphin-colony.r: The colony was small, poorly supplied and frequently mutinous, relying on [[e:cattle|cattle]] and [[e:rice|rice]] obtained from the Antanosy by trade or raiding. Etienne de Flacourt, governor from 1648 to 1655, wrote a detailed history of Madagascar. Colonists also settled [[s:ile-bourbon|Bourbon]] (Reunion), and the post came under the new [[e:french-east-india-company|French East India Company]] in 1664.
fort-dauphin-colony.e: Mounting conflict with the Antanosy culminated in an attack in 1674, after which the surviving French evacuated to [[s:ile-bourbon|Bourbon]] and [[e:india|India]]. [[e:france|France]] later used the episode to justify its claims to Madagascar.

french-protectorate-of-tonkin.t: Northern Vietnam under French rule from 1884, the most populous part of Indochina and the heartland of the Vietnamese independence movement.
french-protectorate-of-tonkin.o: French expeditions to the Red River delta in the 1870s and 1880s, against Vietnamese forces and Chinese Black Flag irregulars, led to the Patenotre Treaty of 1884, which made northern [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]], Bac Ky, a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]]. The Sino-French War of 1884 to 1885 ended Qing claims to the region.
french-protectorate-of-tonkin.r: Nominally under the Nguyen emperor, [[s:trinh-lords|Tonkin]] was in practice run directly by a French résident supérieur in [[e:hanoi|Hanoi]], which became the capital of [[s:french-indochina|French Indochina]] in 1902. [[e:france|France]] built the Long Bien bridge, the Yunnan railway and mines at Hon Gai, but heavy taxes, monopolies on salt and alcohol, and labour recruitment caused hardship. The delta was the main base of nationalist and communist organisations.
french-protectorate-of-tonkin.e: [[e:japan|Japan]] occupied the region from 1940 and ended French rule in March 1945. A famine in 1944 to 1945 killed perhaps a million people. In August 1945 the [[e:viet-minh|Viet Minh]] seized [[e:hanoi|Hanoi]], and Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the [[s:democratic-republic-of-vietnam|Democratic Republic of Vietnam]].

free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.t: Smallest north German republic of the Weimar era, the successor of the grand duchy, merged with its neighbour by the Nazis.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.o: Grand Duke Adolf Frederick VI died in February 1918 without a direct heir, leaving the throne in dispute. After the November revolution a state council took over, and Mecklenburg-Strelitz became a free state, adopting a constitution in 1919 and ending the archaic feudal constitution of 1755.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.r: The free state was a parliamentary republic with a Landtag elected by universal suffrage, governed from Neustrelitz. It remained rural, poor and sparsely populated, with large estates, and included the detached district of Ratzeburg. Its small size made it financially weak, and governments alternated between Social Democrats and conservative parties.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.e: After the Nazi seizure of power the Landtag was dissolved. On 1 January 1934 a Reich law merged it with the [[s:free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin|Free State of Mecklenburg-Schwerin]] into the [[s:free-state-of-mecklenburg|Free State of Mecklenburg]].

fukuoka-domain.t: The Kuroda domain of Chikuzen in northern Kyushu, which shared with Saga the duty of guarding Nagasaki.
fukuoka-domain.o: Kuroda Nagamasa, son of Hideyoshi's strategist Kuroda Kanbei, fought for [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] at [[e:battle-of-sekigahara|Sekigahara]] and received Chikuzen province in 1600 with about 520,000 koku. He built Fukuoka castle beside the old merchant city of Hakata.
fukuoka-domain.r: The Kuroda ruled for the whole [[e:edo-period|Edo period]]. The twin cities of [[e:samurai|samurai]] Fukuoka and merchant Hakata formed one of Kyushu's largest urban centres. From 1641 the domain alternated with Saga in guarding [[e:nagasaki|Nagasaki]], [[e:japan|Japan's]] only port for [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and Chinese trade. The Confucian scholar Kaibara Ekken served the domain, and Kuroda Nagahiro promoted Western learning in the 19th century.
fukuoka-domain.e: Fukuoka joined the imperial side in 1868. In 1870 its officials were found counterfeiting money, and the last lord, Kuroda Nagatomo, was dismissed in 1871 shortly before the domains were abolished; it became Fukuoka Prefecture.

french-indochina.t: France's federation of colonies and protectorates in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, its most valuable Asian possession for nearly seventy years.
french-indochina.o: In 1887 [[e:france|France]] grouped [[s:french-cochinchina|French Cochinchina]], the [[e:protectorate|protectorates]] of [[s:french-protectorate-of-annam|Annam]] and [[s:french-protectorate-of-tonkin|Tonkin]], and the [[s:french-protectorate-of-cambodia|French protectorate of Cambodia]] into the Indochinese Union. The [[s:french-protectorate-of-laos|French protectorate of Laos]] was added after 1893 and the leased territory of [[s:guangzhouwan|Guangzhouwan]] in [[e:china|China]] in 1898. Governor-General Paul Doumer centralised its government around 1900.
french-indochina.r: A governor-general in [[e:hanoi|Hanoi]] controlled a common budget financed by monopolies on opium, salt and alcohol. [[e:france|France]] built railways, ports and the University of Hanoi, and promoted [[e:rice|rice]] exports, [[e:rubber|rubber]] and [[e:coal|coal]] mining. A small Vietnamese elite was educated in French, while peasants bore heavy taxes. Nationalist and communist movements, including the Indochinese Communist Party founded in 1930, grew in opposition.
french-indochina.e: [[s:vichy-france|Vichy France]] allowed Japanese troops in from 1940, and [[e:japan|Japan]] ended French rule in March 1945. [[e:france|France]] returned and fought the [[e:viet-minh|Viet Minh]] in the First [[e:indochina|Indochina]] War. Defeat at [[e:battle-of-dien-bien-phu|Dien Bien Phu]] and the [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]] Accords of 1954 ended French Indochina.

fuladu.t: A Fula kingdom in the upper Casamance, founded by Alfa Molo after the fall of Kaabu, whose son Musa Molo played Britain and France against each other.
fuladu.o: Fuladu arose from a revolt of [[e:fula|Fula]] herders and dependants against the [[e:mandinka|Mandinka]] rulers of the [[s:kaabu-empire|Kaabu Empire]]. Their leader [[e:alfa-molo-balde|Alfa Molo]], with support from the [[s:imamate-of-futa-jallon|Imamate of Futa Jallon]], took part in the wars that destroyed [[e:kaabu-empire|Kaabu's]] capital [[e:kansala|Kansala]] in 1867, and he built a new kingdom in the upper Casamance and the upper [[e:the-gambia|Gambia]] valley.
fuladu.r: [[e:alfa-molo-balde|Alfa Molo's]] son Musa Molo, who ruled from about 1881, ruthlessly expanded the kingdom from his capital Hamdallai, with an army of [[e:fula|Fula]] fighters and captives. He traded with British merchants on the [[e:the-gambia|Gambia]] and French ones in [[e:senegal|Senegal]], signing treaties with both and gaining arms. Fuladu lived by farming, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and raiding.
fuladu.e: The Anglo-French border cut through Fuladu, and Musa Molo's position weakened as both powers tightened control. In 1903 he burned his capital and fled into the [[s:gambia-colony-and-protectorate|Gambia Colony and Protectorate]], and his lands were divided between [[s:french-senegal|French Senegal]], the [[e:the-gambia|Gambia]] and [[s:portuguese-guinea|Portuguese Guinea]].

free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.t: A small Allgäu linen town that remained a free imperial city for five centuries, until the German mediatisation of 1802.
free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.o: Leutkirch grew up as the market centre of the Nibelgau in upper Swabia. In 1293 it received the town law of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-lindau|Lindau]] from King Adolf of [[s:county-of-nassau|Nassau]], and it came to rank as a free imperial city answerable only to the emperor, although the imperial bailiwick over the surrounding countryside was often pledged to neighbouring lords.
free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.r: A small council-governed town, Leutkirch lived from weaving linen and from the market of the surrounding farms. It adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 1540s, and its Protestant [[e:burghers|burghers]] coexisted uneasily with Catholic neighbours such as the local abbeys and the [[s:county-of-waldburg|County of Waldburg]]. It sat in the Swabian Circle and on the Swabian bench of cities at the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]].
free-imperial-city-of-leutkirch.e: The town suffered repeatedly in the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]]. In 1802, as the mediatisation of the imperial cities began, Bavaria occupied it, and in 1810 it passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]]. Today it is Leutkirch im Allgäu in Baden-Württemberg.

french-india.t: France's scattered settlements in India, centred on Pondicherry, which under Dupleix briefly challenged Britain for mastery of the south.
french-india.o: The [[e:french-east-india-company|French East India Company]] was founded in 1664. It set up a factory at [[e:surat|Surat]] in 1668, and in 1674 Francois Martin founded Pondicherry on land granted by the [[s:bijapur-sultanate|Bijapur Sultanate]]. Further settlements followed at Chandernagore in [[e:bengal|Bengal]], Mahe on the Malabar coast, Karaikal and Yanam.
french-india.r: Pondicherry became a planned town with a European quarter and Tamil quarters, ruled by a governor. Joseph-Francois Dupleix, governor from 1742, intervened in the succession disputes of the [[s:carnatic-sultanate|Carnatic Sultanate]] and Hyderabad, raising Indian troops and briefly dominating the [[e:deccan|Deccan]], until Robert Clive's victories reversed French fortunes. The Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] in 1763 restricted [[e:france|France]] to unfortified trading posts.
french-india.e: The settlements were repeatedly occupied by [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and restored after 1815. Chandernagore joined [[e:india|India]] after a 1949 plebiscite, and Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam were transferred de facto in 1954, legally in 1962. They form the Union Territory of Puducherry.

french-saint-lucia.t: French-settled island of the Windwards that changed hands between France and Britain about fourteen times before Britain kept it in 1814.
french-saint-lucia.o: After failed English attempts in 1605 and 1639, settlers sent by Jacques Dyel du Parquet of [[s:colony-of-martinique|Martinique]] established a French post on [[s:saint-lucia|Saint Lucia]] in 1650 and reached an accommodation with the Kalinago. [[e:france|France]] claimed the island continuously thereafter, though [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] disputed it, and for long periods it was declared neutral and left to the Kalinago and a few settlers.
french-saint-lucia.r: [[s:saint-lucia|Saint Lucia]] was governed as a dependency of [[s:colony-of-martinique|Martinique]]. Its fine harbour, Le Carénage, renamed Castries in 1785 after the naval minister, made it strategically valuable, and its slopes were planted with [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] and [[e:cacao|cacao]] by settlers and enslaved Africans, mostly after 1763. During the Revolution, [[e:slavery|slavery]] was abolished in 1794 and Saint Lucia saw fierce fighting between republicans and the British.
french-saint-lucia.e: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] captured the island again in 1803 and the Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] of 1814 ceded it to [[e:britain|Britain]], creating the [[s:colony-of-saint-lucia|Colony of Saint Lucia]]. French law, place names, [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] and the French-based Kwéyòl language remained a lasting legacy of the French period.

franks.t: A confederation of Germanic peoples on the lower Rhine whose kings conquered Gaul and founded the realm from which France and Germany both grew.
franks.o: The [[e:frankish-kingdom|Franks]] ('the bold' or 'the free') appear in Roman sources around 250, a grouping of older Rhineland peoples such as the Chamavi, Chattuarii, [[s:bructeri|Bructeri]] and [[s:sugambri|Sugambri]]. They raided Gaul by land and sea, while many served as Roman soldiers. In 358 Julian allowed the [[s:salian-franks|Salian Franks]] to settle in Toxandria, in the modern [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]] and [[s:kingdom-of-belgium|Belgium]].
franks.r: The confederation was led by many petty kings, with [[s:salian-franks|Salian Franks]] in the north-west and [[s:kingdom-of-cologne|Rhineland Franks]] around [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]]. [[e:frankish-kingdom|Franks]] rose high in Roman service, among them the generals Arbogast and Bauto. The grave of King Childeric I at Tournai, found in 1653, shows a ruler wearing both a Roman officer's cloak brooch and Frankish weapons.
franks.e: In 481 Childeric's son [[e:clovis-i|Clovis I]] became king and united the Frankish groups, defeating the Roman ruler Syagrius in 486 and converting to Catholic [[e:christianity|Christianity]]. His Merovingian kingdom, [[s:kingdom-of-the-franks|Francia]], absorbed the [[s:alemanni|Alemanni]] and [[s:kingdom-of-the-thuringians|Thuringians]] and passed later to the [[e:carolingian-empire|Carolingians]], whose divisions produced [[s:east-francia|East Francia]] and [[e:france|France]].

fante-confederacy.t: An alliance of Fante states on the Gold Coast that drafted a modern written constitution in 1871, an early landmark of African self-government.
fante-confederacy.o: In 1867-1868 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] exchanged forts on the [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast]], placing some Fante towns under Dutch control, while the [[s:ashanti-empire|Ashanti Empire]] threatened invasion. Fante kings and educated Fante met at Mankessim in 1868 and formed a confederacy to coordinate defence and resist the transfer, besieging Dutch-allied [[e:elmina|Elmina]].
fante-confederacy.r: In 1871 the confederacy adopted the Mankessim Constitution, which provided for a king-president, an executive council, an assembly of kings and chiefs, a poll tax, schools, roads and the development of agriculture and mining. Its leaders included the king-president Ghartey IV of Winneba and Western-educated men such as James Hutton Brew. It sought cooperation with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] but also self-government.
fante-confederacy.e: The British saw the confederacy as a challenge, arrested its leaders in 1871 and refused recognition. It faded by 1873, and in 1874 the area became part of the [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast Colony]]. Ghanaian nationalists later saw it as a forerunner.

free-imperial-city-of-aalen.t: A small imperial city at the edge of the Swabian Jura, built beside the largest Roman cavalry fort on the Raetian limes.
free-imperial-city-of-aalen.o: Aalen stands beside the largest Roman cavalry fort north of the [[e:alps|Alps]], built in the 2nd century on the Raetian limes. The medieval town was founded around 1240 under the Hohenstaufen. After a period pledged to the counts of [[s:county-of-oettingen|Oettingen]], it was recognised as a free imperial city by [[e:charles-iv|Charles IV]] in 1360.
free-imperial-city-of-aalen.r: One of the smallest imperial cities, Aalen was governed by a council and lived from crafts, farming, trade and iron ore mined nearby. It adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in 1575 and belonged to the Swabian Circle. A great fire in 1634, during the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]], destroyed much of the town.
free-imperial-city-of-aalen.e: In 1802 and 1803 Aalen was annexed by Württemberg, becoming part of the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]] in 1806. Today it is a city in Baden-Württemberg, and its Limes Museum stands on the site of the Roman fort.

federated-malay-states.t: British-controlled federation of four Malay sultanates, the economic heart of colonial Malaya built on tin and rubber.
federated-malay-states.o: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] had placed residents at the courts of [[s:perak-sultanate|Perak]], the [[s:selangor-sultanate|Selangor Sultanate]], the [[s:pahang-sultanate|Pahang Sultanate]] and the states of [[s:negeri-sembilan|Negeri Sembilan]] from 1874 onwards. In 1895 these were combined into the Federated Malay States, under a Resident-General in Kuala Lumpur, the first being Frank Swettenham, to unify administration, finance and railways.
federated-malay-states.r: The sultans kept their thrones and authority over [[e:islam|Islam]] and Malay custom, but British officials ran government. Chinese-run [[e:tin|tin]] mines and European [[e:rubber|rubber]] estates worked by Indian labourers made the federation one of the most profitable parts of the empire. Railways, roads and towns spread, and a Federal Council was set up in 1909.
federated-malay-states.e: [[e:japan|Japan]] occupied the states from 1942 to 1945. In 1946 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] merged them with the [[s:unfederated-malay-states|Unfederated Malay States]], [[s:prince-of-wales-island|Penang]] and [[e:malacca|Malacca]] into the [[s:malayan-union|Malayan Union]], replaced in 1948 by the [[s:federation-of-malaya|Federation of Malaya]].

first-hellenic-republic.t: The provisional Greek state of the War of Independence, from the constitution of Epidaurus in 1822 to the arrival of a king in 1832.
first-hellenic-republic.o: In January 1822 the First National Assembly at [[s:epidaurus|Epidaurus]] declared Greek independence and adopted a provisional constitution, uniting the regional governments such as the [[s:peloponnesian-senate|Peloponnesian Senate]]. Alexandros Mavrokordatos was elected president of the executive. The new state controlled the Peloponnese, parts of the mainland and many islands.
first-hellenic-republic.r: Divided between notables, islanders and military chiefs, the government fell into civil war in 1823-1825 just as Ibrahim Pasha's Egyptian army invaded. The intervention of [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], [[e:france|France]] and [[e:russia|Russia]] at [[e:battle-of-navarino|Navarino]] in 1827 saved the revolution. Ioannis Kapodistrias, elected governor, arrived in 1828 and built a central administration at Nauplia, founding schools and a currency, the phoenix.
first-hellenic-republic.e: The [[e:london|London]] Protocol of 1830 recognised Greek independence. Kapodistrias was assassinated at Nauplia in October 1831, and chaos followed. In 1832 the great powers chose Otto of Bavaria as king, creating the [[s:kingdom-of-greece|Kingdom of Greece]].

french-senegal.t: France's oldest colony in sub-Saharan Africa, which grew from a trading post at Saint-Louis into the political centre of French West Africa.
french-senegal.o: French merchants founded Saint-Louis in 1659 on an island at the mouth of the [[e:senegal|Senegal]] river, and [[e:france|France]] took [[s:goree|Goree]] from the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] in 1677. [[e:chartered-company|Chartered companies]] traded upriver for gum arabic, gold and slaves, with forts as far as [[s:kingdom-of-gajaaga|Galam]]. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] occupied the posts during wars in 1758-1779 and 1809-1817 before they returned to France.
french-senegal.r: Louis Faidherbe, governor in 1854-1861 and 1863-1865, pushed French rule inland, fought the [[s:toucouleur-empire|Toucouleur Empire]] and [[s:cayor|Cayor]], and founded Dakar. The Four Communes of Saint-Louis, [[s:goree|Goree]], Rufisque and Dakar gave their inhabitants French citizenship, and in 1914 they elected Blaise Diagne, the first black African in the French parliament. [[e:groundnut|Groundnuts]] became the main export, and [[e:sufism|Sufi]] brotherhoods such as the Mourides shaped rural society.
french-senegal.e: [[e:senegal|Senegal]] became an autonomous republic within the [[e:french-community|French Community]] in 1958, joined the [[e:mali|Mali]] Federation in 1959, and became fully independent on 20 August 1960 under Leopold Sedar Senghor. Dakar, capital of [[s:french-west-africa|French West Africa]], remained the capital of the new state.
french-senegal.re: Sunni Islam (Sufi orders), Catholicism among settlers

french-dahomey.t: The French colony built on the conquered Kingdom of Dahomey, known for its educated elite as the Latin Quarter of Africa, which became independent in 1960.
french-dahomey.o: [[e:france|France]] had [[e:protectorate|protectorates]] at [[s:kingdom-of-porto-novo|Porto-Novo]] and on the coast from the 1860s. After wars with the [[s:kingdom-of-dahomey|Kingdom of Dahomey]] in 1890 and 1892, General Alfred-Amedee Dodds took Abomey, and King Behanzin surrendered in 1894. That year the colony of [[e:kingdom-of-dahomey|Dahomey]] and dependencies was formed, with [[e:porto-novo|Porto-Novo]] as its capital, and French forces extended it north to the [[e:niger-river|Niger]].
french-dahomey.r: The colony, part of [[s:french-west-africa|French West Africa]], exported [[e:palm-oil|palm oil]] and palm kernels from the south. Mission schools produced a large educated class, and Dahomeans served as clerks and teachers across French [[e:west-africa|West Africa]], earning the colony the nickname the [[e:latin|Latin]] Quarter of [[e:africa|Africa]]. Politics after 1946 was divided along regional lines, led by Sourou Migan Apithy, Hubert Maga and Justin Ahomadegbe.
french-dahomey.e: [[s:kingdom-of-dahomey|Dahomey]] became an autonomous republic in 1958 and independent on 1 August 1960, with Maga as president. Years of coups followed, and in 1975 the country was renamed the People's Republic of [[e:benin-empire|Benin]].

french-second-republic.t: The short republic of 1848 that introduced universal male suffrage and abolished slavery, then elected the president who would overthrow it.
french-second-republic.o: The [[e:february-revolution|February Revolution]] of 1848 toppled the [[s:july-monarchy|July Monarchy]]. A provisional government including the poet Alphonse de Lamartine proclaimed the Republic, introduced [[e:universal-suffrage|universal male suffrage]], abolished [[e:slavery|slavery]] in the colonies under Victor Schoelcher's decree, and created National Workshops for the unemployed.
french-second-republic.r: The elected assembly was conservative, and the closure of the National Workshops provoked the June Days uprising, crushed by General Cavaignac with thousands killed. In December 1848 Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, nephew of [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]], was elected president by a landslide. The assembly then restricted suffrage and passed the Falloux law strengthening Church schools.
french-second-republic.e: Barred from a second term, Louis-Napoléon staged a coup on 2 December 1851, approved by plebiscite. A year later, on 2 December 1852, he proclaimed himself Emperor [[e:napoleon-iii|Napoleon III]], founding the [[s:second-french-empire|Second French Empire]].

free-state-of-fiume.t: Internationally recognised independent city-state around the port of Fiume, created to settle the dispute between Italy and Yugoslavia and annexed by Italy in 1924.
free-state-of-fiume.o: The Treaty of Rapallo, signed by [[e:italy|Italy]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-yugoslavia|Kingdom of Yugoslavia]] in November 1920, created the Free State of Fiume as a compromise over the disputed port. After Italian forces ended D'Annunzio's [[s:italian-regency-of-carnaro|Italian Regency of Carnaro]] in January 1921, elections in April 1921 were won by the Autonomist Party of Riccardo Zanella, who favoured independence.
free-state-of-fiume.r: Zanella's government struggled with economic collapse, as the port had lost its Hungarian hinterland, and with violent opposition from Italian nationalists and Fascists. In March 1922 a Fascist coup drove Zanella into exile, and Italian military authorities effectively took over. The population was mainly Italian, Croatian and Hungarian.
free-state-of-fiume.e: By the Treaty of [[e:rome|Rome]] in January 1924, [[e:italy|Italy]] and [[e:yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]] partitioned the territory: Italy annexed Fiume, while Yugoslavia received the neighbouring Sušak district. After the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] the city became Rijeka in Yugoslavia, and most Italians left.

french-first-republic.t: The revolutionary republic that executed a king, fought most of Europe, passed through the Terror and the Directory, and ended in Napoleon's empire.
french-first-republic.o: After the storming of the Tuileries in August 1792, a newly elected National Convention abolished the monarchy of the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]] on 21 September 1792 and proclaimed the Republic. Louis XVI was tried and executed in January 1793, while French armies fought [[e:austria|Austria]], [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]].
french-first-republic.r: Facing war and revolt, the Convention gave power to the Committee of Public Safety under Robespierre; the Terror executed thousands before his fall in July 1794. The Directory governed from 1795 amid corruption and coups. The Republic introduced the metric system, abolished feudal dues and [[e:slavery|slavery]] in 1794, and conquered [[s:kingdom-of-belgium|Belgium]], the Rhineland and [[e:italy|Italy]].
french-first-republic.e: [[e:napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]] seized power in the coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 and governed as First [[e:consul|Consul]], restoring order through the Concordat of 1801 and the Civil Code. In May 1804 the Republic was transformed into the [[s:french-empire|First French Empire]].

free-imperial-city-of-cologne.t: The largest city of medieval Germany, which broke free of its archbishops at Worringen in 1288 and stayed a Catholic imperial city until the French came in 1794.
free-imperial-city-of-cologne.o: [[e:cologne|Cologne]] grew from the Roman colony of Colonia Agrippina and was ruled for centuries by its archbishops. Its [[e:burghers|burghers]] fought them repeatedly, and the decisive victory came at the Battle of Worringen in 1288, after which the archbishops could no longer reside in the city. Emperor Frederick III formally confirmed its imperial status in 1475.
free-imperial-city-of-cologne.r: After 1396 the Verbundbrief gave political power to 22 [[e:guild|guild]]-like associations. [[e:cologne|Cologne]] was the largest German city of the Middle Ages, a leading Hanseatic member trading wine, cloth and metalwork. Its citizens founded a university in 1388, and the cathedral, begun in 1248 to house the shrine of the Three Kings, drew pilgrims. Cologne remained firmly Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-cologne.e: French revolutionary troops occupied [[e:cologne|Cologne]] in 1794, and it was annexed to [[e:france|France]]. In 1815 it passed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] and became the main city of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] Province. The cathedral was completed in 1880 and is a World Heritage Site.

free-imperial-city-of-friedberg.t: Wetterau imperial city that shared its hill with a powerful imperial castle, whose knights gradually took control of the town.
free-imperial-city-of-friedberg.o: The Hohenstaufen emperors built a castle and founded a town at Friedberg on a ridge in the Wetterau, the town being documented as an imperial city in 1211. It lay on the trade route from [[e:frankfurt|Frankfurt]] to the north and held important fairs in the 13th century.
free-imperial-city-of-friedberg.r: The city council governed the [[e:burghers|burghers]], but the castle's [[s:burgraviate-of-friedberg|Burgraviate of Friedberg]] next door constantly competed with it. Friedberg joined the Wetterau city league with [[e:frankfurt|Frankfurt]], [[s:free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar|Wetzlar]] and [[s:free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen|Gelnhausen]]. Cloth making and trade made it prosperous until the 14th century, and its Jewish community built a deep ritual bath around 1260 that survives. Debts and decline later left the town largely under the castle's influence.
free-imperial-city-of-friedberg.e: The city was pledged in 1455 and gradually dominated by the Burgraviate. It adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] and kept nominal imperial status until 1802, when it passed to [[s:grand-duchy-of-hesse|Hesse-Darmstadt]]. It is now a town in Hesse.

francoist-spain.t: The dictatorship of Francisco Franco, born in the Spanish Civil War and lasting until his death in 1975.
francoist-spain.o: After the military coup of July 1936 against the [[s:second-spanish-republic|Second Spanish Republic]], the rebel generals named Francisco Franco head of state and Generalísimo at Burgos on 1 October 1936. Backed by [[s:nazi-germany|Nazi Germany]] and Fascist [[e:italy|Italy]], his Nationalists won the civil war in April 1939.
francoist-spain.r: Franco ruled through the army, the Church and a single party, FET y de las JONS, with harsh repression, executions and labour camps in the 1940s. [[e:spain|Spain]] stayed out of the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]], apart from sending the Blue Division to [[e:russia|Russia]]. Cold War alliance with the [[s:united-states|United States]] in 1953 ended isolation, and the Stabilisation Plan of 1959 brought rapid growth, tourism and urbanisation.
francoist-spain.e: In 1969 Franco named Juan Carlos de Borbón as his successor. ETA killed Prime Minister Luis Carrero Blanco in 1973. Franco died on 20 November 1975, and Juan Carlos became king, opening the transition to the democratic [[s:kingdom-of-spain|Kingdom of Spain]].

free-state-of-the-isthmus.t: Panama's first attempt at independence, a breakaway state from New Granada that lasted about a year during the War of the Supremes.
free-state-of-the-isthmus.o: Civil war, the War of the Supremes, broke out in the [[s:republic-of-new-granada|Republic of New Granada]] in 1839. In November 1840 a popular assembly in [[s:republic-of-panama|Panama]] City, cut off from Bogotá, declared the provinces of Panama and Veraguas independent as the State of the Isthmus, choosing Colonel Tomás Herrera as head of state.
free-state-of-the-isthmus.r: Herrera's government adopted a constitution in 1841, maintained order and sought to protect the isthmus's transit trade between the Atlantic and Pacific, on which its merchants depended. It considered recognition from foreign powers and the possibility of a federal link with New [[e:granada|Granada]] on its own terms.
free-state-of-the-isthmus.e: When the civil war ended, the government of New [[e:granada|Granada]] negotiated Panama's return with promises of greater autonomy. The isthmus was reincorporated on 31 December 1841. The episode was a precedent for Panama's independence in 1903, and Herrera is honoured as a national figure.

free-county-of-burgundy.t: Franche-Comté, the imperial county of Burgundy across the Saône, rich in salt and fiercely loyal to its Habsburg rulers until Louis XIV conquered it.
free-county-of-burgundy.o: Otto-William, a grandson of Berengar of [[e:italy|Italy]], gathered the counties east of the Saône in the 980s and founded the comital house. The county lay in the [[s:kingdom-of-arles|Kingdom of Arles]] and so in the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], unlike the neighbouring [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Duchy of Burgundy]], which was a French fief.
free-county-of-burgundy.r: Salt springs at Salins and Lons-le-Saunier provided the county's wealth, and a parliament sat at Dole. Countess Beatrice married [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] in 1156, tying the county to the Hohenstaufen. Through marriage it passed to Philip the Bold in 1384 and joined the [[s:burgundian-state|Burgundian State]], then went with Mary of [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] to the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] and the Spanish crown.
free-county-of-burgundy.e: [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]] invaded in 1668 and again in 1674. The Treaty of Nijmegen in 1678 gave the county to the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]], which moved its capital to [[s:imperial-city-of-besancon|Besançon]]. Its lasting name, Franche-Comté, recalls its separate past.

french-west-africa.t: The federation of eight French colonies governed from Dakar, which for six decades ruled a territory larger than Western Europe.
french-west-africa.o: [[e:france|France]] created the federation in 1895 to coordinate its expanding conquests, placing [[s:french-senegal|French Senegal]], [[s:french-sudan|French Sudan]], [[s:french-guinea|French Guinea]] and the [[s:french-ivory-coast|French Ivory Coast]] under a governor-general at Saint-Louis. The seat moved to Dakar in 1902, and Ernest Roume reorganised the federation in 1904. [[s:french-dahomey|French Dahomey]], [[e:mauritania|Mauritania]], the [[s:colony-of-niger|Colony of Niger]] and [[s:french-upper-volta|French Upper Volta]] were added as they were formed.
french-west-africa.r: Each colony had a governor, but the federation ran customs, railways, defence and the budget. Africans outside the Four Communes were subjects under the indigenat code, liable to forced labour and summary punishment, while the Ecole William Ponty trained an African elite. The federation supplied about 200,000 [[e:tirailleurs|tirailleurs]] senegalais in the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]]. In 1940 it sided with Vichy and repelled the [[s:free-france|Free French]] at Dakar before joining the [[e:allies|Allies]] in 1942.
french-west-africa.e: After 1946 Africans gained citizenship and seats in the French parliament, and the 1956 framework law gave power to the territories. The federation was dissolved in 1958-1959, and its members became independent in 1960, except [[e:guinea|Guinea]] in 1958.

french-sudan.t: The French colony on the upper and middle Niger, conquered by military campaigns from 1880, which became independent as Mali in 1960.
french-sudan.o: French officers began the conquest of the upper [[e:senegal|Senegal]] and [[e:niger-river|Niger]] in 1880 as the military territory of the Upper River, pushing east from [[s:french-senegal|French Senegal]]. Commanders such as Gustave Borgnis-Desbordes, Joseph Gallieni and Louis Archinard built forts at Kita and Bamako in 1883 and defeated the [[s:toucouleur-empire|Toucouleur Empire]], Samori Toure's [[s:wassoulou-empire|Wassoulou Empire]] and [[s:kenedougou-kingdom|Kenedougou]] by 1898.
french-sudan.r: The territory changed name several times, becoming Upper [[e:senegal|Senegal]] and [[e:niger-river|Niger]] in 1904 and French [[e:sudan|Sudan]] in 1920, with its capital at Bamako from 1908. It was part of [[s:french-west-africa|French West Africa]]. The Dakar-Niger railway linked it to the coast, and the Office du Niger, founded in 1932, built irrigation works for [[e:cotton|cotton]] and [[e:rice|rice]] using forced labour. Most of the population were Muslim farmers and herders.
french-sudan.e: Modibo [[e:keita-dynasty|Keita's]] Sudanese Union led the territory to autonomy as the Sudanese Republic in 1958. It joined [[e:senegal|Senegal]] in the [[e:mali|Mali]] Federation in 1959; after Senegal withdrew, it declared independence as Mali on 22 September 1960.

french-grenada.t: French colony on Grenada, founded after a brutal conquest of its Kalinago inhabitants, that grew sugar and cacao until Britain took it in the Seven Years' War.
french-grenada.o: Jacques Dyel du Parquet, governor of [[s:colony-of-martinique|Martinique]], bought rights to [[s:grenada|Grenada]] and landed with settlers in 1649, founding a fort at the site of St George's. War with the Kalinago followed; in 1651 the last defenders reportedly leapt from a cliff in the north, remembered as Le Morne des Sauteurs. Du Parquet sold the island to the Comte de Cérillac in 1657.
french-grenada.r: [[s:grenada|Grenada]] came under the French West [[e:india|India]] Company in 1664 and the crown in 1674, administered as a dependency of [[s:colony-of-martinique|Martinique]]. Fort Royal guarded a fine natural harbour. Settlers developed [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]], [[e:cacao|cacao]] and [[e:indigo|indigo]] estates worked by enslaved Africans, and by the 1750s the colony had dozens of sugar mills. [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] was the only permitted faith.
french-grenada.e: British forces captured [[s:grenada|Grenada]] in 1762, and the Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] of 1763 ceded it to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], beginning the [[s:colony-of-grenada|Colony of Grenada]]. [[e:france|France]] retook it in 1779 but returned it in 1783. French place names, Catholic parishes and a French-based [[e:criollo-people|Creole]] survive from this period.

cr.a: See file history below for details.

french-equatorial-africa.t: The federation of France's colonies in central Africa, governed from Brazzaville, and the first part of the empire to rally to de Gaulle.
french-equatorial-africa.o: In 1910 [[e:france|France]] grouped its central African territories into a federation modelled on [[s:french-west-africa|French West Africa]]: [[s:gabon-french-colony|Gabon]], [[s:middle-congo|Middle Congo]] and [[s:ubangi-shari|Ubangi-Shari]], with [[e:chad|Chad]] separated as a colony in 1920. A governor-general ruled from [[e:brazzaville|Brazzaville]], while each colony kept a lieutenant-governor.
french-equatorial-africa.r: The federation was the poorest part of the French empire. Concession companies, compulsory [[e:cotton|cotton]] growing, [[e:timber|timber]] extraction and forced labour, notably for the Congo-Ocean railway, provoked revolts such as the Kongo-[[e:wara|Wara]] rising in [[s:ubangi-shari|Ubangi-Shari]]. In August 1940 Félix Éboué, governor of [[e:chad|Chad]] and later governor-general, led the federation to join [[s:free-france|Free France]], and the 1944 [[e:brazzaville|Brazzaville]] Conference promised reforms.
french-equatorial-africa.e: After 1946 its peoples became French citizens and elected deputies. In 1958 the four territories became autonomous republics within the [[e:french-community|French Community]] and the federation was dissolved, its members becoming independent in August 1960.

fujian-peoples-government.t: A short-lived rebel government in Fuzhou, set up in 1933 by the 19th Route Army in protest at Chiang Kai-shek's policy of appeasing Japan.
fujian-peoples-government.o: The 19th Route Army, famous for defending Shanghai against [[e:japan|Japan]] in 1932, was moved to Fujian to fight the Communists. Its commanders Cai Tingkai and Jiang Guangnai, with the Nationalist dissidents Li Jishen and Chen Mingshu, broke with Chiang Kai-shek and in November 1933 proclaimed the People's Revolutionary Government of the [[s:republic-of-china|Republic of China]] at Fuzhou.
fujian-peoples-government.r: The government rejected the Kuomintang, adopted a new flag and a programme of resistance to [[e:japan|Japan]], land reform and opposition to Chiang. It concluded a preliminary agreement with the [[s:chinese-soviet-republic|Chinese Soviet Republic]], but the Communist leadership gave no real military help, and other regional leaders also stayed aloof.
fujian-peoples-government.e: Chiang moved large forces against Fujian, and the rebellion collapsed in January 1934 after only two months. The 19th Route Army was broken up, and its leaders fled to [[e:hong-kong|Hong Kong]], later joining the anti-Japanese struggle.

free-imperial-city-of-offenburg.t: Ortenau imperial city at the mouth of the Kinzig valley, often pledged to neighbours and burned by the French in 1689.
free-imperial-city-of-offenburg.o: Offenburg grew at the crossing of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] valley road and the Kinzig valley into the Black Forest, under the dukes of Zähringen. After their line died out in 1218, it fell to the Hohenstaufen and by the 1240s was treated as an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-offenburg.r: The town was governed by a council and lived from its market, crafts and the Kinzig [[e:timber|timber]] trade. With the rest of the Ortenau it was repeatedly pledged by the emperors to neighbouring lords, including the [[e:bishop|bishops]] of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]] and the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Palatinate]], which limited its independence. After a brief Protestant phase it remained Catholic. French troops burned the town in 1689 during the Nine Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-offenburg.e: Offenburg lost its freedom in 1803 and was annexed by Baden. In 1847 the Offenburg Programme of the democratic movement was proclaimed there. It is now a town in Baden-Württemberg.

further-austria.t: The Habsburgs' scattered western lands in Swabia, Alsace and the Breisgau, governed for four centuries from Ensisheim and Freiburg.
further-austria.o: The [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] came from the [[s:county-of-habsburg|County of Habsburg]] in Aargau and held scattered lands across Swabia, Alsace and the upper [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. The Treaty of Neuberg of 1379 divided the family's possessions, giving the western territories, together with Tyrol and [[s:inner-austria|Inner Austria]], to Leopold III; these western lands became known as Further [[e:austria|Austria]].
further-austria.r: Further [[e:austria|Austria]] was a patchwork: the Breisgau with Freiburg, the Sundgau in Alsace, the forest towns on the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], the margraviate of [[s:margraviate-of-burgau|Burgau]] and the county of Hohenberg. It was governed from Ensisheim and later Freiburg, often together with the [[s:county-of-tyrol|County of Tyrol]], and had its own estates. Heavy losses to the Swiss followed in the 15th century. The University of Freiburg was founded in 1457.
further-austria.e: The [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] gave the Alsatian lands to [[e:france|France]] in 1648. After the Peace of Pressburg in 1805 the remaining territories were divided among the [[s:grand-duchy-of-baden|Grand Duchy of Baden]], the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]], ending [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] rule in south-west [[e:germany|Germany]].

free-city-of-frankfurt.t: Self-governing city-republic on the Main that hosted the German Federal Diet and the 1848 Frankfurt Parliament.
free-city-of-frankfurt.o: [[e:frankfurt|Frankfurt]], a free imperial city for centuries and the place of imperial elections and coronations, had been part of Dalberg's [[s:grand-duchy-of-frankfurt|Grand Duchy of Frankfurt]]. The [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] restored it in 1815 as one of four [[e:free-imperial-city|free cities]] of the [[s:german-confederation|German Confederation]], and a constitution was adopted in 1816.
free-city-of-frankfurt.r: The city was governed by a senate and legislative assembly dominated by its wealthy Lutheran citizens. It was the seat of the Federal Diet and a major banking centre, home of the Rothschild bank. In 1848-49 the [[e:frankfurt|Frankfurt]] Parliament, the first freely elected German national assembly, met in St Paul's Church and drafted a constitution for a united [[e:germany|Germany]].
free-city-of-frankfurt.e: [[e:frankfurt|Frankfurt]] sided with [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1866. Prussian troops occupied it, imposed a heavy indemnity, and the city was annexed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] within the Province of Hesse-Nassau; its mayor, Karl Fellner, took his own life.

free-state-of-schaumburg-lippe.t: One of Germany's smallest republics, a successor of the Bückeburg principality that resisted absorption until 1946.
free-state-of-schaumburg-lippe.o: Prince Adolf II of [[s:principality-of-schaumburg-lippe|Schaumburg-Lippe]] abdicated on 15 November 1918, and the principality became a free state, with a constitution adopted in 1922 and Bückeburg as capital.
free-state-of-schaumburg-lippe.r: With around 50,000 inhabitants, the state was largely rural, with sandstone quarrying and [[e:coal|coal]] mining at Obernkirchen. Proposals to merge with [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] failed in the 1920s, and the state kept its small parliament until the Nazis took power and placed it under a Reich governor shared with Lippe. Its tiny size made it a symbol of German particularism.
free-state-of-schaumburg-lippe.e: After 1945 it was in the British zone, and in November 1946 it was merged with Hanover, Brunswick and [[s:county-of-oldenburg|Oldenburg]] into Lower Saxony. The former princely family still lives at Bückeburg Palace, and the district of Schaumburg preserves the name.

french-mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.t: The League of Nations mandate under which France governed Syria and Lebanon between the world wars, shaping both modern states.
french-mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.o: The San Remo conference of April 1920 assigned [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and [[s:lebanese-republic|Lebanon]] to [[e:france|France]]. French forces overthrew the [[s:arab-kingdom-of-syria|Arab Kingdom of Syria]] at Maysalun that July, and the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] formally confirmed the mandate in 1923.
french-mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.r: [[e:france|France]] ruled through a high commissioner in [[s:beirut|Beirut]] and divided the territory into [[s:greater-lebanon|Greater Lebanon]], the states of [[e:damascus|Damascus]] and [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]], the [[s:alawite-state|Alawite State]], the [[s:jabal-druze-state|Jabal Druze State]] and the [[s:sanjak-of-alexandretta|Sanjak of Alexandretta]], often favouring minorities. The Great Syrian Revolt of 1925-1927, led by [[e:sultan|Sultan]] al-Atrash, was crushed after French artillery shelled Damascus. A 1936 treaty promising independence was never ratified by France, and in 1939 Alexandretta was ceded to [[e:turkey|Turkey]].
french-mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.e: After British and [[s:free-france|Free French]] forces took the territories from [[s:vichy-france|Vichy France]] in 1941, independence was proclaimed. [[s:lebanese-republic|Lebanon]] gained real control in 1943, and the last French troops left [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] in April and [[e:lebanon|Lebanon]] in December 1946.
french-mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.re: Sunni Islam, Christianity, Alawite and Druze communities

cr.a: Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon

free-imperial-city-of-nuremberg.t: Franconian imperial city of Dürer and Hans Sachs, keeper of the imperial regalia and one of the great trading and craft centres of early modern Europe.
free-imperial-city-of-nuremberg.o: [[e:nuremberg|Nuremberg]] grew around an imperial castle first recorded in 1050 on a sandstone ridge above the Pegnitz. Its merchants gained privileges from the Salian and Hohenstaufen emperors, and in 1219 [[e:frederick-ii|Frederick II's]] Great Charter of Freedom laid the basis for its self-government, gradually freeing it from the Hohenzollern burgraves who held the castle.
free-imperial-city-of-nuremberg.r: A closed circle of patrician families ran the council, excluding [[e:guild|guilds]] from power. Metalwork, instruments, weapons and long-distance trade made the city rich, and from 1424 to 1796 it kept the imperial regalia. Albrecht Dürer, Veit Stoss, Hans Sachs and Martin Behaim, maker of the oldest surviving globe, worked there. [[e:nuremberg|Nuremberg]] turned Lutheran in 1525 and won a large rural territory in the Landshut War of 1504 to 1505.
free-imperial-city-of-nuremberg.e: War, debts and shifting trade routes weakened the city after 1600. In 1806 it was annexed by the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]]. It became a major industrial centre, and its old town was largely destroyed in 1945 and rebuilt.

first-empire-of-haiti.t: The first independent state created by formerly enslaved people, ruled by Emperor Jacques I, the revolutionary general Jean-Jacques Dessalines.
first-empire-of-haiti.o: After defeating [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] army at Vertières in November 1803, [[e:jean-jacques-dessalines|Jean-Jacques Dessalines]] proclaimed the independence of [[s:republic-of-haiti|Haiti]] at Gonaïves on 1 January 1804, reviving the island's Taíno name. In September 1804 he took the title of emperor, in conscious rivalry with Napoleon, and was crowned as Jacques I in October.
first-empire-of-haiti.r: Dessalines ruled as a military autocrat from Marchand, his fortified capital in the Artibonite. In early 1804 he ordered the killing of most remaining French whites. The 1805 constitution banned white property ownership, declared all Haitians black and made the state the owner of much former plantation land. To revive exports, he forced labourers back onto plantations under military supervision, which caused growing resentment.
first-empire-of-haiti.e: Land reviews that threatened the property of the mixed-race elite, combined with harsh labour rules, provoked a conspiracy. Dessalines was ambushed and killed at Pont-Rouge near Port-au-Prince on 17 October 1806. [[s:republic-of-haiti|Haiti]] then split between Henri Christophe's [[s:state-of-haiti|State of Haiti]] in the north and Alexandre Pétion's [[s:republic-of-haiti-1806-1849|Republic of Haiti]] in the south.
