french-saint-christophe.t: France's first lasting colony in the Caribbean, on Saint Kitts, base for the settlement of Guadeloupe and Martinique.
french-saint-christophe.o: The Norman captain Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc landed on Saint Christopher in 1625 and, with the backing of Cardinal Richelieu's Compagnie de Saint-Christophe, founded a French colony. In 1627 the French and English partitioned the island, the French taking the two ends, including Basseterre.
french-saint-christophe.r: French Saint-Christophe grew tobacco and later [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], worked by indentured servants and enslaved Africans. From here d'Esnambuc launched the settlement of [[s:colony-of-martinique|Martinique]] in 1635. Philippe de Longvilliers de Poincy, governor-general of the French Antilles from 1639, ruled from a grand château on the island and bought it for the Knights of Malta in 1651.
french-saint-christophe.e: The French and English repeatedly expelled each other during the wars of the late 17th century. By the [[e:treaty-of-utrecht|Treaty of Utrecht]] in 1713 [[e:france|France]] ceded its share to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], merging it into the [[s:colony-of-saint-christopher|Colony of Saint Christopher]].

free-imperial-city-of-obernai.t: Alsatian wine town below Mont Sainte-Odile, birthplace of Alsace's patron saint and a member of the Decapolis league of imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-obernai.o: Obernai lies at the foot of Mont Sainte-Odile and is held to be the birthplace of Saint Odile, patron saint of Alsace. A Hohenstaufen town, it was recognised as an imperial city in the 1280s, around 1283, and in 1354 it joined the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-obernai.r: A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] ruled this prosperous small town, which lived from wine, grain and crafts. Its market square, town hall and corn hall reflect late medieval and [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] prosperity. Obernai remained Catholic during the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]]. Like the other [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]] cities, it suffered heavily during the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years War]].
free-imperial-city-of-obernai.e: After the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] gave [[e:france|France]] rights in Alsace, French troops occupied the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], and the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679 confirmed French rule. Obernai is now a town in Alsace, France.

free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.t: A Neckar wine and trading city whose imperial charter of 1371 made it a self-governing republic of burghers until 1802.
free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.o: Heilbronn grew around a royal estate at a Neckar crossing, first mentioned in 741. The town received a charter from Rudolf I in 1281, and in 1371 [[e:charles-iv|Charles IV]] granted it a constitution that confirmed its status as a free imperial city and gave power to a council drawn from patricians and guildsmen.
free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.r: Heilbronn lived from Neckar shipping, which it controlled through its weir, and from vineyards. The city accepted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in 1528 under the preacher Johann Lachmann. The knight Götz von Berlichingen was held prisoner in its tower in 1519, and in 1633 [[e:sweden|Sweden]] and the Protestant estates concluded the Heilbronn League there.
free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.e: Heilbronn was annexed by Württemberg in 1802 and became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]] in 1806. Heavily bombed in December 1944, it was rebuilt and is now an industrial and wine centre in Baden-Württemberg.

free-state-of-waldeck.t: Small Hessian republic, successor of the Principality of Waldeck-Pyrmont, which gave up its independence in stages to Prussia.
free-state-of-waldeck.o: Prince Friedrich of [[s:principality-of-waldeck|Waldeck-Pyrmont]] was deposed in November 1918, and the principality became a free state with Arolsen as capital. Waldeck had been administered by [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] under an accession treaty since 1868, so its independence was already limited.
free-state-of-waldeck.r: The free state was rural and poor, with farming and forestry in the hills around the Eder. Its finances depended on Prussian support. In 1921 the inhabitants of the detached district of [[s:county-of-pyrmont|Pyrmont]] voted to join [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], and Pyrmont passed to the Province of Hanover in 1922. The remaining state struggled to sustain its own government.
free-state-of-waldeck.e: After a treaty with [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], the Free State of Waldeck was absorbed into Prussia on 1 April 1929 and became part of the Province of Hesse-Nassau. It is now in the state of Hesse.

free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.t: One of the smallest Alsatian Decapolis cities, a wine town known for its Romanesque church of Saints Peter and Paul.
free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.o: Rosheim, at the foot of the Vosges west of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]], was an imperial possession under the Hohenstaufen. The town was walled in the 13th century and its rights as a free imperial city were confirmed around 1303. In 1354 it joined the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], the alliance of ten Alsatian imperial cities under the imperial bailiff at [[s:free-imperial-city-of-haguenau|Haguenau]].
free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.r: A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] governed this small community of vintners, farmers and craftsmen. Its church of Saints Peter and Paul, built in the 12th century of yellow sandstone, is one of the finest Romanesque buildings in Alsace, and the town also preserves a stone house of the same age. Rosheim remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.e: The town suffered heavily in the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]]. After 1648 the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]] came under French protection, and the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1679 confirmed its incorporation into the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]]. It is now a small town in the Bas-Rhin [[e:departement|department]].

french-madagascar.t: Madagascar as a French colony, from the overthrow of the Merina monarchy to the autonomous Malagasy Republic of 1958.
french-madagascar.o: After the conquest of 1895 and the end of the [[s:french-protectorate-of-madagascar|French Protectorate of Madagascar]], [[e:france|France]] annexed the island in 1896. In February 1897 the governor-general Joseph Gallieni abolished the Merina monarchy and exiled Queen Ranavalona III to [[e:algeria|Algeria]], then put down the Menalamba rising and subdued the coastal peoples.
french-madagascar.r: Gallieni and his successors imposed a head tax and forced labour, promoted French over English schooling and broke the power of the Merina elite. [[e:coffee-economy|Coffee]], vanilla, [[e:cloves|cloves]] and [[e:rice|rice]] were exported, and [[s:nosy-be|Nosy Be]], [[s:diego-suarez-colony|Diego-Suarez]] and the Comoros were attached. In 1942 British forces took the island from [[s:vichy-france|Vichy France]], and it passed to the [[s:free-france|Free French]].
french-madagascar.e: The nationalist uprising of 1947 was crushed with tens of thousands of deaths. Madagascar became the autonomous Malagasy Republic in October 1958 and fully independent on 26 June 1960 under President Philibert Tsiranana.

former-shu.t: The kingdom founded in Sichuan by the soldier Wang Jian, a wealthy refuge for Tang scholars and poets in the turmoil after the Tang collapse.
former-shu.o: Wang Jian, a soldier from Henan who had served in the palace army, seized Chengdu in 891 and became military governor of the region. The [[s:later-tang|Tang]] made him Prince of Shu in 903. When [[e:zhu-wen|Zhu Wen]] deposed the Tang in 907, Wang Jian refused to recognise the [[s:later-liang|Later Liang]] and proclaimed himself emperor.
former-shu.r: Protected by mountains, the fertile [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] basin escaped the wars of the north and prospered from [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:silk|silk]], salt and [[e:tea|tea]]. Many [[s:later-tang|Tang]] officials and literati took refuge at Chengdu, among them the poet Wei Zhuang, who served as chief minister. The Huajian anthology of song lyrics was compiled there in 940, after the dynasty, but reflects the court culture it fostered.
former-shu.e: Wang Jian's son Wang Yan, who succeeded in 918, was extravagant and neglected government. In 925 a [[s:later-tang|Later Tang]] army marched in and met little resistance; Wang Yan surrendered and was killed with his family in 926 on the way to [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]]. [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] soon became independent again as [[s:later-shu|Later Shu]].

frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.t: Merovingian kingdom of the Rhône and Saône valleys, built on the old Kingdom of the Burgundians and ruled from Chalon-sur-Saône.
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.o: The [[s:franks|Franks]] conquered the [[s:kingdom-of-the-burgundians|Kingdom of the Burgundians]] in 534. At the division of 561 Chlothar I's son Guntram received [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] with Orléans, ruling from Chalon-sur-Saône. The kingdom stretched from the Loire to the [[e:alps|Alps]] and the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]].
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.r: Guntram, a long-reigning king later venerated as a saint, acted as mediator between his feuding brothers' kingdoms. [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] kept its [[e:roman-law|Roman law]] and Gallo-Roman aristocracy and its own mayor of the palace. The Irish monk Columbanus founded Luxeuil there, but was expelled by King Theuderic II and Brunhild.
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.e: After 613 [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] was ruled together with [[s:neustria|Neustria]] by Chlothar II and his successors, though it kept a separate identity. It passed under Pippinid control, and [[e:charles-martel|Charles Martel]] subdued it in the 730s. With Pippin's accession in 751 it became a region of the Frankish realm.

free-state-bottleneck.t: Accidental mini-state in the Rhine valley, left unoccupied between French and American zones after the First World War.
free-state-bottleneck.o: The [[e:armistice-of-11-november-1918|armistice]] of 1918 gave the [[e:allies|Allies]] bridgeheads on the right bank of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], drawn as circles of 30 kilometres around Koblenz and [[e:mainz|Mainz]]. The two circles left a narrow gap near Lorch and Kaub, cut off from unoccupied [[e:germany|Germany]] by hills, which became known from January 1919 as the Free State Bottleneck.
free-state-bottleneck.r: The area of some 17,000 people had no direct road or rail link with [[e:germany|Germany]]. Lorch's mayor, Edmund Pnischeck, headed an improvised administration. Locals smuggled goods across the hills, printed their own emergency money and, in a famous episode, hijacked a French [[e:coal|coal]] train to keep warm.
free-state-bottleneck.e: During the occupation of the Ruhr, French troops occupied the territory in February 1923, ending its separate existence. The area returned to German administration when the French occupation was later lifted.

frisian-freedom.t: A medieval coastal society without lords, in which Frisian farmers governed themselves through elected judges and assemblies for nearly four centuries.
frisian-freedom.o: After the Carolingian counts lost effective control of the [[e:north-sea|North Sea]] coast in the 11th and 12th centuries, the Frisian lands between the Vlie and the Weser governed themselves. [[s:frisii|Frisians]] claimed their liberty came from a privilege granted by [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]], a legend that justified their refusal to accept feudal lords.
frisian-freedom.r: Each land or community chose its own judges, called redjeven or consuls, and delegates of the Seven Sealands met at the Upstalsboom near Aurich. [[s:frisii|Frisians]] built dykes and terps, raised [[e:cattle|cattle]] and traded by sea, and wrote down their own laws in Old Frisian. There were no knights or castles in the usual sense, but powerful chieftains, the hoofdelingen, rose in the 14th century.
frisian-freedom.e: Feuds between the Schieringers and Vetkopers weakened the [[s:frisii|Frisians]] in the 15th century. East Frisia came under the Cirksena counts in 1464, and in 1498 Emperor Maximilian made Albert of Saxony governor of [[s:lordship-of-frisia|Friesland]], ending the freedom west of the Ems and creating the Lordship of Frisia.

free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.t: Swabian imperial city, perhaps the oldest Hohenstaufen town, home of the Parler family of master builders and long famous for gold and silver work.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.o: Gmünd is often called the oldest Hohenstaufen town, founded around 1162 near the family's ancestral castle on the Hohenstaufen hill. After the execution of Conradin, the last Hohenstaufen, in 1268, the town was not claimed by any prince and became an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.r: A council of patricians and later [[e:guild|guilds]] governed the city. Heinrich Parler began the Holy Cross Minster there in the 14th century, one of the first German hall churches in the late Gothic style, and his son Peter Parler went on to build [[e:prague|Prague]] Cathedral. Gold and [[e:silver|silver]] smithing and the making of rosaries were its main trades. Gmünd remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.e: The city lost its freedom in 1802, when Württemberg annexed it. It remains a centre of the goldsmith's and silversmith's trade and is now a town in Baden-Württemberg, with the Holy Cross Minster at its heart.

free-imperial-city-of-lindau.t: Island city in Lake Constance, a trading gateway to Italy and Switzerland and one of four cities that signed the Tetrapolitan Confession in 1530.
free-imperial-city-of-lindau.o: Lindau grew around a convent of noble canonesses founded on an island in Lake Constance. The town became an important market and port, and after the Hohenstaufen era it gained recognition as an imperial city, around 1275, gradually limiting the convent's rights.
free-imperial-city-of-lindau.r: A council of patricians and [[e:guild|guilds]] governed. Lindau thrived on trade over the lake and through the Alpine passes to [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]], served by the Lindau messenger service. The city hosted an [[e:imperial-diet|imperial diet]] in 1496. It accepted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] and in 1530 joined [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]], Constance and [[s:free-imperial-city-of-memmingen|Memmingen]] in presenting the Tetrapolitan Confession, later adopting [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]].
free-imperial-city-of-lindau.e: In 1802 Lindau went to Prince Bretzenheim, then to [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1804 and to Bavaria in 1805. It remains Bavarian, Bavaria's only town on Lake Constance, linked to the mainland by bridge and railway causeway.

free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.t: Swabian imperial city of the Fugger and Welser bankers, where the Augsburg Confession was read in 1530 and the Peace of Augsburg made in 1555.
free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.o: [[e:augsburg|Augsburg]] grew from the Roman provincial capital of Augusta Vindelicorum and was ruled for centuries by its [[e:bishop|bishops]]. Its citizens won increasing self-government, and in 1276 King Rudolf I confirmed their town law, making Augsburg an imperial city independent of the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-augsburg|Prince-Bishopric of Augsburg]].
free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.r: A council of patricians and [[e:guild|guilds]] governed after the guild revolution of 1368. Textile production and banking made [[e:augsburg|Augsburg]] one of [[e:europe|Europe's]] richest cities; the [[e:fugger-family|Fuggers]] financed emperors and founded the Fuggerei social housing in 1516. The Augsburg Confession was presented at the diet of 1530, and the [[e:peace-of-augsburg|Peace of Augsburg]] of 1555 recognised [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]]. After 1648 Catholics and Protestants shared offices equally.
free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.e: [[e:augsburg|Augsburg]] lost its freedom in 1806 when it was annexed by the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]]. It remains a major Bavarian city, and the Peace Festival of 8 August, held since 1650, is still a local holiday.

free-state-of-saxony.t: Republican Saxony between the monarchy and East German centralisation, an industrial state of left-wing politics and later Soviet rule.
free-state-of-saxony.o: King Frederick [[e:augustus-iii|Augustus III]] abdicated in November 1918, and workers' and soldiers' councils briefly took power. A Landtag was elected in 1919, and in 1920 a constitution established Saxony as a free state within the [[s:weimar-republic|Weimar Republic]], with Dresden as capital.
free-state-of-saxony.r: Saxony's industry made it a stronghold of the Social Democrats and Communists. In 1923 the government of Erich Zeigner, including Communists, was deposed by the federal government with troops. The Nazis took control in 1933, with Martin Mutschmann as Reich governor. Dresden was devastated by Allied bombing in February 1945, and Saxony fell in the Soviet occupation zone.
free-state-of-saxony.e: After 1945 Saxony was restored as a Land in the Soviet zone and in 1949 in the German Democratic Republic. In 1952 the GDR abolished the Länder, dividing Saxony into the districts of Dresden, Leipzig and Chemnitz (renamed Karl-Marx-Stadt in 1953); it was re-established in 1990.

free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.t: Lake Constance imperial city whose grain market fed the region and whose walls held off Swedish sieges in the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.o: Überlingen was a royal estate and Hohenstaufen town on the north shore of Lake Constance, with a harbour serving the grain trade across the lake. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen around 1268, it became an imperial city, confirmed by later kings, with a small territory of nearby villages.
free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.r: A council dominated by [[e:guild|guilds]] ruled. Its grain market supplied [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]] and the lake region, and wine was another source of wealth. The town remained Catholic and loyal to the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]], and in 1632 and 1634 it withstood Swedish sieges. Its large Gothic minster of St. Nicholas holds a famous carved high altar by Jörg Zürn.
free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.e: Überlingen lost its freedom in 1803 when it was annexed by Baden. In the 19th century its mineral spring made it a spa and resort town, and it is now in Baden-Württemberg, its minster and walls well preserved.

four-macedonian-republics.t: The four self-governing districts into which Rome split the old kingdom of Macedon after Pydna, a short-lived experiment that ended in revolt and annexation.
four-macedonian-republics.o: After defeating Perseus at Pydna in 168 BCE, [[e:rome|Rome]] abolished the [[s:antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia|Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia]]. In 167 BCE Lucius Aemilius Paullus announced the settlement at [[s:amphipolis|Amphipolis]]: [[e:kingdom-of-macedon|Macedon]] was to be 'free' but divided into four republics (merides) with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, [[s:pella|Pella]] and Pelagonia.
four-macedonian-republics.r: Each republic had elected magistrates and a council, but contact between them was restricted: citizens could not marry or own land across the borders. The [[e:macedonian-empire|Macedonians]] paid [[e:rome|Rome]] half the taxes they had paid their kings, the royal gold and [[e:silver|silver]] mines were closed until 158 BCE and [[e:timber|timber]] from the royal forests was banned. The first meris struck silver coins showing Artemis.
four-macedonian-republics.e: Resentment and disorder grew. In 149 BCE Andriscus, claiming to be a son of Perseus, reunited [[e:kingdom-of-macedon|Macedon]] briefly as king. Quintus Caecilius Metellus defeated him in 148 BCE, and Macedonia became a Roman province in 146 BCE, with the Via Egnatia later binding it together.

falerii.t: Chief city of the Faliscans, a people who spoke a language close to Latin but lived within Etruscan culture, destroyed by Rome in 241 BCE.
falerii.o: Falerii, later called Falerii Veteres, stood on a steep tufa plateau at modern Civita Castellana in the Ager Faliscus, between the [[e:tiber-river|Tiber]] and Monte Cimino. It developed from Iron Age settlements of the 9th and 8th centuries BCE. The Faliscans spoke Faliscan, an Italic language closely related to [[e:latin|Latin]], though their art, cults and politics were tied to Etruria.
falerii.r: Falerii was famous for the cult of Juno Curitis, whose festival Ovid described, and for its temples decorated with fine terracottas. Its workshops produced Faliscan red-figure vases in the 4th century BCE. The city usually allied with [[s:veii|Veii]] against [[e:rome|Rome]]; Roman legend tells how Camillus, besieging it in 394 BCE, sent back a schoolmaster who tried to hand over his pupils, and the Faliscans surrendered in admiration.
falerii.e: After further wars Falerii revolted in 241 BCE, just after the [[e:first-punic-war|First Punic War]], and was crushed within days. [[e:rome|Rome]] destroyed the hilltop city and moved its people to Falerii Novi on open ground about 6 km away, whose walls still stand. The old site was resettled in the Middle Ages as Civita Castellana.

free-state-of-icaria.t: Tiny independent republic declared on the Aegean island of Icaria in 1912 after islanders expelled the Ottoman garrison, lasting months until union with Greece.
free-state-of-icaria.o: Icaria, a mountainous island west of [[s:principality-of-samos|Samos]], was under Ottoman rule when [[e:italy|Italy's]] war with the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] weakened Turkish control in the [[e:aegean|Aegean]]. On 17 July 1912 the islanders, led by the doctor Ioannis Malachias, rose against the small Ottoman garrison, forced its surrender and proclaimed the Free State of Icaria.
free-state-of-icaria.r: The new state set up a provisional government at Agios Kirykos, adopted its own flag and issued postage stamps. It lacked money, an army and any outside recognition, and the islanders, who lived by farming, herding and emigration, hoped for annexation by [[e:greece|Greece]] rather than lasting independence.
free-state-of-icaria.e: When the First Balkan War began, the Greek navy arrived in November 1912 and the island joined the [[s:kingdom-of-greece|Kingdom of Greece]]. The episode lasted about five months and is still commemorated on Icaria every July.

free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.t: Democratic successor of the Kingdom of Württemberg, a well-governed Weimar state that was split by the occupying powers in 1945.
free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.o: In November 1918 King William II abdicated, and a provisional government of Social Democrats and Independents declared a republic in Stuttgart. A constitution adopted in 1919 created the Free People's State of Württemberg.
free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.r: Württemberg had a balanced economy of small farms and skilled industry, with companies such as Bosch and Daimler. After governments led by Social Democrats and liberals, the state was led by conservatives and from 1928 by the Centre's Eugen Bolz, who was later executed for his part in the resistance to Hitler. After 1933 the Nazi Reich governor Wilhelm Murr ruled the state.
free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.e: After 1945 the state was divided by the occupying powers: the northern part, in the American zone, joined northern Baden as Württemberg-Baden, and the southern part, under the French, became Württemberg-Hohenzollern. They merged into Baden-Württemberg in 1952.

funj-sultanate.t: The Sultanate of Sennar, which replaced Christian Alodia and ruled the middle Nile for three centuries, spreading Islam across Sudan.
funj-sultanate.o: In 1504 the Funj leader Amara Dunqas founded [[e:funj-sultanate-of-sennar|Sennar]] on the Blue [[e:nile|Nile]]. Allied with the Arab chief Abdallah Jamma of the [[s:abdallab-sheikhdom|Abdallab Sheikhdom]], the Funj destroyed [[s:alodia|Alodia]] and its capital Soba, establishing a sultanate that dominated the Gezira and the Nile valley north to the third cataract.
funj-sultanate.r: The sultan ruled through [[e:vassal|vassal]] lords, among them the [[s:abdallab-sheikhdom|Abdallab]], who held the north. [[e:funj-sultanate-of-sennar|Sennar]] grew rich on gold, slaves and caravan trade with [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]]. [[e:sufism|Sufi]] teachers and Islamic schools spread [[e:islam|Islam]] and Arabic among the population. Badi II created a slave army, and later sultans were dominated by the Hamaj regents from 1761.
funj-sultanate.e: Weakened by civil wars, [[e:funj-sultanate-of-sennar|Sennar]] fell to Ismail Pasha's army in 1821 as [[s:egypt-under-muhammad-ali|Egypt under Muhammad Ali]] conquered [[e:sudan|Sudan]], creating the [[s:turco-egyptian-sudan|Turco-Egyptian Sudan]]. The last sultan, Badi VII, submitted without a fight.

free-state-of-anhalt.t: Small central German republic that hosted the Bauhaus at Dessau and in 1932 became the first state with a Nazi head of government.
free-state-of-anhalt.o: Duke Joachim Ernst's regent abdicated in November 1918, and the [[s:duchy-of-anhalt|Duchy of Anhalt]] became a free state, with a democratic constitution adopted in 1919 and Dessau as capital.
free-state-of-anhalt.r: [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]] was governed by Social Democratic coalitions for most of the 1920s. Its industries included the Junkers aircraft works and chemical plants at Bitterfeld nearby. In 1925 the Bauhaus moved from Weimar to Dessau, where Walter Gropius designed its new building. After the Nazis won the 1932 state election, Alfred Freyberg became the first Nazi minister-president of a German state, and the Bauhaus was forced out that year.
free-state-of-anhalt.e: The Nazis subordinated [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]] to a Reich governor. In 1945 it was occupied and placed in the Soviet zone, where it was merged with the Prussian Province of Saxony to form the province, later Land, of Saxony-Anhalt.

free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.t: Tiny imperial city on the north shore of Lake Constance that was merged with a neighbouring priory to form the town of Friedrichshafen in 1811.
free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.o: Buchhorn grew on the north shore of Lake Constance as a fishing and market settlement under the counts of Buchhorn and later the Guelphs and Hohenstaufen. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen it was recognised as an imperial city by Rudolf I around 1275.
free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.r: Buchhorn was one of the smallest imperial cities, with a council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] and a tiny territory. It lived from fishing, lake shipping and trade across the lake to [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]], and its market served the surrounding countryside. It remained Catholic and depended on alliances with other Swabian cities and on Austrian goodwill.
free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.e: Bavaria annexed Buchhorn in 1802 and passed it to Württemberg in 1810. In 1811 King Frederick I of Württemberg merged it with the neighbouring Hofen priory to create Friedrichshafen, later the home of the Zeppelin airships.

french-protectorate-of-tunisia.t: Tunisia under French rule from 1881, where the bey reigned but a French resident-general governed, until independence in 1956.
french-protectorate-of-tunisia.o: Using border raids as a pretext, [[e:france|France]] invaded the [[s:beylik-of-tunis|Beylik of Tunis]] in 1881 and forced Muhammad as-Sadiq Bey to sign the Treaty of Bardo. The La Marsa Convention of 1883 placed internal administration under French control, with the bey retained as nominal sovereign.
french-protectorate-of-tunisia.r: A French resident-general held real power, with French officials running finance, public works and justice for Europeans. French and Italian settlers acquired farmland for olives, vines and grain, and phosphate mining expanded. Tunisian nationalism grew through the Destour party, founded in 1920, and Habib Bourguiba's Neo-Destour from 1934. Moncef Bey was deposed by the French in 1943.
french-protectorate-of-tunisia.e: After armed resistance and negotiations, [[e:france|France]] granted internal autonomy in 1955 and full independence in March 1956. Lamine Bey became king of the [[s:kingdom-of-tunisia|Kingdom of Tunisia]], with Bourguiba as prime minister.

fib.t: A Pictish province between the Tay and the Forth, the ancestor of the Kingdom of Fife, named in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne.
fib.o: Fib appears among the seven Pictish provinces named after the legendary sons of Cruithne. Its territory corresponded broadly to modern Fife and Kinross, between the Firth of Tay and the Firth of Forth.
fib.r: Nothing is known of its rulers in the Pictish period. The peninsula was fertile, and St Andrews, known earlier as Cennrigmonaid, became one of the leading Pictish churches, receiving relics of Saint Andrew by tradition in the 8th century.
fib.e: Fib became the earldom of Fife within the [[s:kingdom-of-scotland|Kingdom of Scotland]], whose earls held the right to enthrone the king at Scone. Fife still calls itself 'the Kingdom'.

free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.t: Swabian imperial city on Roman foundations, seat of an imperial court and for over a century an ally of the Swiss Confederacy.
free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.o: Rottweil grew on the site of the Roman town of Arae Flaviae on the upper Neckar. A royal estate in the Carolingian period, it was refounded by the Zähringen and Hohenstaufen and became an imperial city after their fall, by around 1268.
free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.r: The city was home to the Imperial Court of Rottweil, which heard cases from across south-western [[e:germany|Germany]]. A council with strong [[e:guild|guild]] participation governed it, and it acquired one of the largest territories of any Swabian imperial city. In 1519 it concluded a perpetual alliance with the [[s:old-swiss-confederacy|Old Swiss Confederacy]], as an associate member. It remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.e: Rottweil lost its freedom in 1802 when Württemberg annexed it, and the imperial court was abolished. Its Swabian-Alemannic carnival, the Fasnet, remains famous, and it is now a town in Baden-Württemberg.

faroese-commonwealth.t: Self-governing Norse community of the Faroe Islands, ruled by its assembly at Tinganes until it came under the Norwegian crown.
faroese-commonwealth.o: Norse settlers reached the Faroe Islands in the early 9th century; the Irish monk Dicuil wrote around 825 that Irish hermits there had been driven out by Northmen raiders. The settlers were farmers and herders, many from western [[e:norway|Norway]], and some with Gaelic links from the British Isles.
faroese-commonwealth.r: The islanders governed themselves through the Alting at Tinganes, in what is now Tórshavn, one of the oldest parliamentary sites in the world. Sheep farming, fowling and fishing supported the population. The Færeyinga saga tells how Sigmundur Brestisson brought [[e:christianity|Christianity]] around 999 for King Olaf Tryggvason, opposed by the chieftain Tróndur í Gøtu.
faroese-commonwealth.e: By about 1035 the islands paid tax to the Norwegian king and became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-norway|Kingdom of Norway]]. They later passed to [[s:denmark-norway|Denmark-Norway]] and remained with [[e:denmark|Denmark]] after 1814. The Løgting still meets in Tórshavn, and the Faroe Islands are a self-governing part of the Danish realm.

first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.t: The first Ibadi state in Oman, an elected imamate centred on Nizwa that set the pattern for Omani religious government for a thousand years.
first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.o: In 751 the Omani Ibadis elected al-Julanda ibn Mas'ud as their first [[e:imam|imam]], but he was killed the next year by an army of the new [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]]. After decades under local chiefs, the [[e:imamate|imamate]] was restored in 793 with the election of Muhammad ibn Affan, followed by Warith ibn Ka'b, and lasted a century.
first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.r: [[e:imam|Imams]] were chosen by the learned and leading men and could be deposed if they broke the law, an ideal of accountable leadership central to Ibadism. Nizwa became the capital and a centre of scholarship. [[e:oman|Oman]] controlled the sea trade of the Gulf through Sohar, while the falaj irrigation channels supported date farming in the interior. al-Salt ibn Malik ruled for over thirty years.
first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.e: The deposition of al-Salt ibn Malik in 886 split Omani scholars into rival schools and led to civil war. In 893 the Abbasid governor of [[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]], Muhammad ibn Nur, invaded, sacked Nizwa and ended the [[e:imamate|imamate]], though Ibadi [[e:imam|imams]] reappeared repeatedly later.

finnish-socialist-workers-republic.t: Red Finland, the revolutionary government that held southern Finland during the civil war of 1918 before its defeat by the Whites and Germany.
finnish-socialist-workers-republic.o: Tensions after independence erupted into civil war in January 1918. On 28 January the Red Guards seized Helsinki, and the Finnish People's Delegation, chaired by Kullervo Manner, took power in the industrial south. In late February it was proclaimed the Finnish Socialist Workers' Republic.
finnish-socialist-workers-republic.r: The Reds controlled the cities and industrial centres of southern [[s:republic-of-finland|Finland]], including Helsinki, Tampere, Turku and Viipuri. Their draft constitution mixed socialist ideas with parliamentary democracy, and they received arms from [[s:russian-sfsr|Soviet Russia]]. Both sides committed terror, and the Red administration struggled with food shortages and military weakness.
finnish-socialist-workers-republic.e: The White army under Mannerheim won the decisive Battle of Tampere in April 1918, while German troops took Helsinki. Red [[s:republic-of-finland|Finland]] collapsed in May, and about 80,000 Reds were held in prison camps, where some 12,000 died. Its leaders fled to [[s:russian-sfsr|Soviet Russia]] and founded the Communist Party of [[e:finland|Finland]].

free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.t: A northern Alsatian imperial city that grew around a powerful Benedictine abbey and joined the Decapolis before passing to France.
free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.o: Wissembourg grew around the Benedictine abbey of Saints Peter and Paul, founded in the 7th century on the Lauter, where the monk Otfrid wrote his [[e:old-high-german|Old High German]] Gospel Harmony in the 9th century. The townspeople slowly freed themselves from the abbot's lordship, and by the early 14th century the town ranked as a free imperial city. In 1354 it was a founding member of the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]].
free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.r: A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] and [[e:guild|guilds]] governed the town, which lived from wine, crafts and the road between [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]] and the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Palatinate]]. The abbey remained a rival authority; it became a provostry in 1524 and was united with the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-speyer|Prince-Bishopric of Speyer]] in 1546. The [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] won a following among the townspeople, while the abbey stayed Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.e: Repeatedly fought over in the 17th century, Wissembourg came under French protection after 1648, and annexation by the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]] was confirmed by the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679. The exiled Polish king Stanisław Leszczyński later lived there. It is now a town in the Bas-Rhin [[e:departement|department]].

free-state-of-prussia.t: Republican Prussia, Germany's largest state and a democratic bulwark under Social Democrats until a coup in 1932.
free-state-of-prussia.o: With William II's abdication in November 1918 the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]] became a republic. A constitution of 1920 created the Free State of [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], covering about three-fifths of [[e:germany|Germany's]] territory and population, from East Prussia to the Rhineland, though it lost territory to [[e:poland|Poland]], [[s:kingdom-of-belgium|Belgium]] and [[e:denmark|Denmark]] under the [[e:treaty-of-versailles|Treaty of Versailles]].
free-state-of-prussia.r: [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] was governed for most of the 1920s by a coalition of Social Democrats, the Catholic Centre and liberals under Minister-President Otto Braun, with a police force loyal to the republic. In July 1932 Chancellor Franz von Papen removed the Prussian government by decree, the Preußenschlag. Under the Nazis, Hermann Göring became minister-president and Prussia lost its separate statehood in practice.
free-state-of-prussia.e: After 1945 [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia's]] eastern territories passed to [[e:poland|Poland]] and the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]], and its Germans were expelled. The [[s:allied-occupied-germany|Allied Control Council]] formally abolished Prussia by Law No. 46 on 25 February 1947.

four-oirat.t: The confederation of western Mongol peoples that rivalled the Chinggisid khans for two centuries and captured a Ming emperor at Tumu in 1449.
four-oirat.o: The [[e:oirats|Oirats]] were forest and steppe peoples of north-western [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]] who had joined the [[s:mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]] early. After the fall of the [[s:yuan-dynasty|Yuan Dynasty]] in 1368 they formed a union of four main groups, usually listed as the Choros, Torghut, Dörbet and [[s:khoshut-khanate|Khoshut]], and challenged the [[s:northern-yuan|Northern Yuan]] khans for leadership of the steppe.
four-oirat.r: The confederation was governed by an assembly of chiefs, and its leaders, not being descendants of [[e:genghis-khan|Genghis Khan]], usually ruled through puppet khans. Toghon and his son Esen built [[e:oirats|Oirat]] power in the 15th century; Esen defeated and captured the Ming emperor Zhengtong at Tumu in 1449 and briefly took the title of khan himself before being killed in 1455.
four-oirat.e: Pushed west by Dayan Khan and Altan Khan, the [[e:oirats|Oirats]] moved towards [[s:dzungar-khanate|Dzungaria]] in the 16th century and adopted Gelug [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]]. In the 1630s the confederation divided into the Dzungar Khanate, the [[s:kalmyk-khanate|Kalmyk Khanate]] on the [[e:volga|Volga]] and the [[s:khoshut-khanate|Khoshut Khanate]] in [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]].

fatagar-sultanate.t: A small medieval Muslim state in central Ethiopia, caught between the Christian emperors and the sultanates of Ifat and Adal.
fatagar-sultanate.o: Fatagar is known from Arabic and Ethiopian sources as a Muslim region lying between [[s:kingdom-of-shewa|Shewa]] and the Awash river, east of modern [[e:addis-ababa|Addis Ababa]]. It appears in the 13th century and became a tributary of the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]] under [[e:amda-seyon-i|Amda Seyon]] in the 14th century.
fatagar-sultanate.r: Little is recorded about its rulers or institutions. It was a farming and trading area on the [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] to [[e:zeila|Zeila]], and its population was partly Muslim and partly Christian, with both mosques and churches. It served at times as a royal camping ground of the emperors.
fatagar-sultanate.e: Fatagar was overrun during the [[e:jihad|jihad]] of [[e:ahmad-ibn-ibrahim-al-ghazi|Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi]] in the 1530s, and [[e:oromo-migrations|Oromo migrations]] in the mid-16th century then swept away the old political order. The name fell out of use as the area became part of [[e:oromo|Oromo]] [[s:kingdom-of-shewa|Shewa]].

fidenae.t: Small town on the Tiber just north of Rome, allied with Veii, which Rome fought for repeatedly and finally destroyed in 426 BCE.
fidenae.o: Fidenae stood on a hill above the left bank of the [[e:tiber-river|Tiber]], about 8 km north of [[e:rome|Rome]], opposite the Etruscan city of [[s:veii|Veii]]. It was a [[e:latin|Latin]] town, though Livy says it had Etruscan connections, and settlement there goes back to the early Iron Age. Its position on the river and the Via Salaria made it strategically vital.
fidenae.r: Little is known of its government. Roman tradition tells of repeated wars from the time of Romulus, as Fidenae shifted between [[e:rome|Rome]] and [[s:veii|Veii]]. In 438 BCE it went over to Lars Tolumnius of Veii and killed Roman envoys; the Roman officer Aulus Cornelius Cossus killed Tolumnius in single combat and dedicated his armour as the spolia opima.
fidenae.e: In 426 BCE the dictator Mamercus Aemilius captured and destroyed Fidenae, and its land became Roman. It survived only as a village; under Tiberius, in 27 CE, the collapse of a wooden amphitheatre there reportedly killed thousands, as [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] records.

free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.t: Danube city of Roman origin, a great medieval trading hub and from 1663 the permanent seat of the Imperial Diet of the Holy Roman Empire.
free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.o: Regensburg grew from the Roman [[e:legion|legionary]] fortress of [[e:castrum|Castra]] Regina and became the seat of the Bavarian dukes and a [[e:bishop|bishop]]. Its merchants traded from [[e:venice|Venice]] to Kiev, and the Stone Bridge over the [[e:danube|Danube]] was built in the 1130s and 1140s. In 1245 [[e:frederick-ii|Frederick II]] granted the city self-government, making it an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.r: Patrician merchant families, whose tower houses still stand, ruled through the council. The [[e:bishop|bishop]], several imperial abbeys and the city shared the town. Trade declined in the 15th century, and Regensburg briefly submitted to Bavaria from 1486 to 1492. It adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1542. From 1663 to 1806 it hosted the Perpetual [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]], the Empire's standing assembly.
free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.e: In 1803 the city became part of the Principality of Regensburg under Karl Theodor von Dalberg, and in 1810 it passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]]. Its medieval old town is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

free-imperial-city-of-speyer.t: A Rhineland cathedral city that hosted imperial diets and the Imperial Chamber Court and gave Protestantism its name in 1529.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.o: Speyer, the Roman Noviomagus, was the burial place of the Salian emperors, whose cathedral rose there from 1030. The [[e:burghers|burghers]] gradually wrested power from the [[e:bishop|bishop]], helped by Henry V's charter of 1111, and in 1294 the bishop gave up most of his remaining rights, leaving the city self-governing under the emperor alone.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.r: Patricians and later the [[e:guild|guilds]] shared power in the council. The city hosted some fifty [[e:imperial-diet|imperial diets]]; at the 1529 diet the Lutheran estates issued the 'protestation' that gave Protestants their name. From 1527 to 1689 the [[e:imperial-chamber-court|Imperial Chamber Court]], the empire's highest court, sat in Speyer. The city turned Lutheran, while the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-speyer|Prince-Bishopric of Speyer]] kept the cathedral Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.e: In 1689 French troops burned Speyer during the Nine Years' War, and the court moved to [[s:free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar|Wetzlar]]. Revolutionary [[e:france|France]] occupied the city in 1792 and annexed it in 1797. After 1816 it was the capital of the Bavarian [[s:electoral-palatinate|Palatinate]], and it now lies in Rhineland-Palatinate.

free-state-of-mecklenburg.t: Mecklenburg reunited by the Nazis in 1934, which after 1945 became a Land of the Soviet zone and the GDR until its abolition in 1952.
free-state-of-mecklenburg.o: On 1 January 1934 a Reich law merged the [[s:free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin|Free State of Mecklenburg-Schwerin]] and the [[s:free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz|Free State of Mecklenburg-Strelitz]] into a single Land of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]], with [[s:county-of-schwerin|Schwerin]] as capital, ending the division that dated from 1701.
free-state-of-mecklenburg.r: Under the Nazis the state was run by Reich governor Friedrich Hildebrandt. Rostock's Heinkel and Arado aircraft works made it a target of Allied bombing. In 1945 it was occupied by Soviet and British forces and placed in the Soviet zone, gaining western [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]] and receiving many expellees. A land reform in 1945 broke up the large estates.
free-state-of-mecklenburg.e: Known as Mecklenburg-Vorpommern until 1947, the Land became part of the German Democratic Republic in 1949. In 1952 it was divided into the districts of [[s:lordship-of-rostock|Rostock]], [[s:county-of-schwerin|Schwerin]] and Neubrandenburg; the state was re-established in 1990 as Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

federal-republic-of-germany.t: Post-war German democracy, founded in the western zones in 1949 and enlarged by reunification in 1990.
federal-republic-of-germany.o: The three western occupation zones were combined, and a parliamentary council drafted the Basic Law, which came into force on 23 May 1949. Konrad Adenauer became the first chancellor, with Bonn as provisional capital, while the Soviet zone became the German Democratic Republic.
federal-republic-of-germany.r: Under the social market economy of Ludwig Erhard, West [[e:germany|Germany]] experienced the Wirtschaftswunder. It joined NATO in 1955 and was a founding member of the European Economic Community in 1957. Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik eased relations with the East. The federal system gives strong powers to the Länder, and a Constitutional Court guards the Basic Law.
federal-republic-of-germany.e: After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the GDR joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990 under Helmut Kohl. Berlin became the capital, and [[e:germany|Germany]] is today the [[e:european-union|European Union's]] most populous member and largest economy.

french-protectorate-of-madagascar.t: The French protectorate imposed on the Merina monarchy of Madagascar, a step between independence and outright colonial conquest.
french-protectorate-of-madagascar.o: [[e:france|France]] fought the [[s:merina-kingdom|Merina Kingdom]] in the Franco-Hova War of 1883-1885. The treaty of December 1885 gave France control over Madagascar's foreign relations, the bay of [[s:diego-suarez-colony|Diego-Suarez]] and a resident-general at Antananarivo, though the Merina government kept internal power.
french-protectorate-of-madagascar.r: Queen Ranavalona III and her prime minister and husband Rainilaiarivony continued to govern through a modernised administration, a Protestant state church and an army. They disputed French claims to a full [[e:protectorate|protectorate]], and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] recognised French rights only in 1890. Debts from the war indemnity weakened the monarchy.
french-protectorate-of-madagascar.e: In 1895 a French expedition marched on Antananarivo, which fell in September. The Menalamba rising followed, and [[e:france|France]] annexed the island in 1896. In February 1897 General Gallieni abolished the monarchy and exiled the queen, making the island the colony of [[s:french-madagascar|French Madagascar]].

french-territory-of-the-afars-and-the-is.t: The last name of France's colony in Djibouti, adopted in 1967 to stress its Afar and Issa peoples, before independence in 1977.
french-territory-of-the-afars-and-the-is.o: After a referendum in March 1967, in which a majority voted to remain French amid protests and allegations of fraud, [[s:french-somaliland|French Somaliland]] was renamed the French Territory of the [[e:afar|Afars]] and the Issas. The name aimed to emphasise the Afar community, which [[e:france|France]] favoured over the Issa [[e:somalis|Somalis]], who were suspected of favouring union with [[s:somalia|Somalia]].
french-territory-of-the-afars-and-the-is.r: [[e:france|France]] governed through a high commissioner and a local government headed by the [[e:afar|Afar]] politician Ali Aref Bourhan. Restrictions on residence in the capital, enforced with a barrier around [[s:djibouti|Djibouti]] city, targeted [[e:somalis|Somali]] migrants. The port and the railway to [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]] remained the economic base, and the French military kept a large garrison. Nationalists such as Hassan Gouled Aptidon pressed for independence, and in 1976 a hostage crisis at Loyada drew world attention.
french-territory-of-the-afars-and-the-is.e: In May 1977 voters overwhelmingly approved independence, and on 27 June 1977 the territory became the [[s:djibouti|Republic of Djibouti]], with Hassan Gouled Aptidon as president.

five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.t: Five fortified Danish towns of the east Midlands, Derby, Leicester, Lincoln, Nottingham and Stamford, that formed the core of Viking rule south of the Humber.
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.o: After the Great Heathen Army partitioned [[s:kingdom-of-mercia|Mercia]] in 877, Danish warbands settled the east Midlands around fortified centres. Each borough was the base of a jarl and his army, controlling the surrounding district, in an area later known as part of the Danelaw.
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.r: The boroughs were military and trading centres that grew into towns, with Danish law, land units and many Scandinavian place-names in -by and -thorpe. They acted together at times, but there is no evidence of a single ruler. The settlers soon adopted [[e:christianity|Christianity]].
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.e: Aethelflaed of [[s:kingdom-of-mercia|Mercia]] and Edward the Elder took Derby, Leicester, Nottingham and Stamford in 917 and 918. After a Norse revival from York, Edmund of [[e:england|England]] recovered the Five Boroughs in 942, an event celebrated in a poem in the Anglo-[[e:saxons|Saxon]] Chronicle. The region kept distinct legal customs into the 11th century.

french-upper-volta.t: The French colony centred on the Mossi kingdoms, abolished in 1932 and recreated in 1947, which became independent in 1960 and is now Burkina Faso.
french-upper-volta.o: [[e:france|France]] had conquered the region in the 1890s, taking [[s:kingdom-of-ouagadougou|Ouagadougou]], capital of the Kingdom of Ouagadougou, in 1896. The lands were first ruled as part of [[s:french-sudan|French Sudan]], and in 1919 the colony of Upper [[e:volta-river|Volta]] was created, with its capital at Ouagadougou and Edouard Hesling as its first governor.
french-upper-volta.r: The colony, part of [[s:french-west-africa|French West Africa]], was densely populated but poor. [[e:france|France]] ruled through the [[e:mossi|Mossi]] kings, including the [[s:kingdom-of-ouagadougou|Mogho]] Naba, and used the colony as a reservoir of labour for railways and for plantations in the [[s:french-ivory-coast|French Ivory Coast]]. In 1932 it was abolished and divided among the [[e:ivory-trade|Ivory]] Coast, [[s:french-sudan|French Sudan]] and the [[s:colony-of-niger|Colony of Niger]], partly to supply labour.
french-upper-volta.e: [[e:mossi|Mossi]] chiefs and politicians lobbied for its restoration, achieved in 1947. Upper [[e:volta-river|Volta]] became an autonomous republic in 1958 and independent on 5 August 1960 under Maurice Yameogo. It was renamed Burkina Faso in 1984.

free-imperial-city-of-frankfurt.t: Main river trading city where German kings were elected and later crowned, famous for its fairs, its Jewish quarter and as birthplace of Goethe.
free-imperial-city-of-frankfurt.o: [[e:frankfurt|Frankfurt]] grew around a Carolingian palace at a ford over the Main. Royal assemblies met there, and its fairs grew into some of the most important in [[e:europe|Europe]]. The citizens gained self-government in the 13th century, and from about 1245 it was treated as an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-frankfurt.r: A patrician council ruled. The [[e:golden-bull-of-1356|Golden Bull of 1356]] made [[e:frankfurt|Frankfurt]] the place of royal elections, and from 1562 coronations also took place in its cathedral. Its autumn fair and book fair drew merchants from across [[e:europe|Europe]]. [[e:jews|Jews]] lived in the walled Judengasse, attacked in the Fettmilch Uprising of 1614. The city turned Lutheran, and Goethe was born there in 1749.
free-imperial-city-of-frankfurt.e: In 1806 [[e:frankfurt|Frankfurt]] lost its freedom to Dalberg, becoming capital of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-frankfurt|Grand Duchy of Frankfurt]]. In 1815 it became a free city, seat of the [[s:german-confederation|German Confederation]] and of the 1848 Frankfurt Parliament. [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] annexed it in 1866.

free-and-independent-state-of-cundinamar.t: A centralist republic around Bogotá that fought rival federalists during Colombia's 'Foolish Fatherland' before the Spanish reconquest.
free-and-independent-state-of-cundinamar.o: After the Bogotá revolution of 20 July 1810, the province of Santa Fe proclaimed the State of Cundinamarca. Its constitution of 1811, under President Jorge Tadeo Lozano, still recognised Ferdinand VII as king. Antonio Nariño, who had translated the Rights of Man in 1794, soon took power and favoured a strong central government.
free-and-independent-state-of-cundinamar.r: Cundinamarca refused to join the federalist [[s:united-provinces-of-new-granada|United Provinces of New Granada]], and the two sides fought a civil war in 1812 and 1813. Nariño repelled a federalist attack on Bogotá in January 1813, and in July Cundinamarca declared full independence from [[e:spain|Spain]]. Nariño then led a campaign against royalists in the south but was captured at Pasto in 1814.
free-and-independent-state-of-cundinamar.e: In December 1814 Simón Bolívar, serving the [[s:dutch-republic|United Provinces]], captured Bogotá and forced Cundinamarca to join the federation. Pablo Morillo's royalist army retook Bogotá in 1816, ending the first period of independence.

free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.t: Town on the Kinzig founded by Frederick Barbarossa, whose imperial palace hosted the 1180 diet that stripped Henry the Lion of his duchies.
free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.o: Emperor [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] founded Gelnhausen in 1170 as a market town, granting it privileges and building an imperial palace on an island in the Kinzig river. It lay on the trade road from [[e:frankfurt|Frankfurt]] to Leipzig. In 1180 the palace hosted the [[e:imperial-diet|imperial diet]] that issued the Gelnhausen Charter, dividing the lands of Henry the Lion.
free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.r: As an imperial city Gelnhausen was governed by a council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] under the emperor's protection, prospering from trade along the road between [[e:frankfurt|Frankfurt]] and the east. Its Marienkirche, with an unusual eastern tower group, and the ruined palace are among the finest Hohenstaufen buildings. The town was too small to defend its autonomy for long once Hohenstaufen power collapsed.
free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen.e: In 1349 King [[e:charles-iv|Charles IV]] pledged the city to the Counts of [[s:county-of-schwarzburg|Schwarzburg]], and the pledge later passed to the Counts of [[s:county-of-hanau-munzenberg|Hanau]] and the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Electoral Palatinate]], which ruled it jointly. It kept a nominal imperial status until 1803, when it went to [[s:electorate-of-hesse|Hesse-Kassel]]. It is now a town in Hesse.

free-imperial-city-of-schweinfurt.t: Imperial city on the Main destroyed in the margrave war of 1554 and birthplace of the Leopoldina, Germany's oldest academy of sciences.
free-imperial-city-of-schweinfurt.o: Schweinfurt grew around a crossing of the Main and was rebuilt after destruction in the 13th century, being recognised as an imperial city around 1254. It lay between the lands of the [[e:bishop|bishops]] of Würzburg and the Hohenzollerns and had to defend its freedom against both.
free-imperial-city-of-schweinfurt.r: A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] ruled, and the town lived from trade on the Main, crafts and wine. It adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in 1542. In the Second Margrave War Margrave Albert Alcibiades of [[s:principality-of-brandenburg-bayreuth|Brandenburg-Kulmbach]] occupied it, and in 1554 his enemies destroyed the city. In 1652 four Schweinfurt physicians founded the academy later known as the Leopoldina.
free-imperial-city-of-schweinfurt.e: Schweinfurt lost its freedom in 1802 when Bavaria annexed it. In the 19th century it became an industrial town known for ball bearings, and it is now in Bavaria. The Leopoldina is [[e:germany|Germany's]] national academy of sciences.

french-guiana.t: France's territory on the South American mainland, once a notorious penal colony and today home to Europe's spaceport at Kourou.
french-guiana.o: French attempts to settle Cayenne began in the early 17th century, including one in 1643 that ended in disaster. In 1664 a lasting settlement was established at Cayenne under Antoine Lefebvre de La Barre. The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and English contested it, but [[e:france|France]] held it from 1676, apart from a Portuguese-Brazilian occupation from 1809 to 1817.
french-guiana.r: The colony produced [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], [[e:spice-trade|spices]] and annatto with enslaved African labour, but the population remained small. The Kourou expedition of 1763 sent some 12,000 settlers, most of whom died of disease. [[e:slavery|Slavery]] was abolished in 1794, restored in 1802 and finally ended in 1848. From 1852 to 1953 the colony held a penal colony, the bagne, including the Îles du Salut, where Alfred Dreyfus was held on Devil's Island. Gold rushes drew prospectors from the 1850s.
french-guiana.e: French Guiana became an overseas [[e:departement|department]] of [[e:france|France]] in 1946. The Guiana Space Centre opened at Kourou in 1968 and now launches European Ariane rockets. Since 2015 it has been a single territorial collectivity, part of the [[e:european-union|European Union]].

free-imperial-city-of-kempten.t: Protestant imperial city that stood beside the Catholic Prince-Abbey of Kempten, two rival states sharing one town until 1803.
free-imperial-city-of-kempten.o: The town of Kempten grew beside the [[s:prince-abbey-of-kempten|Prince-Abbey of Kempten]], which originally held lordship over it. The [[e:burghers|burghers]] gained growing autonomy, and in 1289 King Rudolf I granted them the rights of an imperial city. Disputes with the abbey continued for centuries.
free-imperial-city-of-kempten.r: A council of [[e:guild|guilds]] and patricians governed the small walled town, which lived from crafts, linen and trade on the Iller. In 1525, in the so-called Great Purchase, the town bought out the abbot's remaining rights over it. It adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]], becoming a Lutheran island beside the Catholic abbey town. Both towns were damaged in the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years War]].
free-imperial-city-of-kempten.e: Bavaria annexed the imperial city in 1802 and the abbey in 1803, and in 1818 the two were united into one town. Kempten is now a Bavarian city, and its old imperial town and abbey quarter remain distinct.

first-philippine-republic.t: Constitutional republic proclaimed at Malolos in 1899, often called the first in Asia, which fought the United States for independence.
first-philippine-republic.o: Following the [[s:revolutionary-government-of-the-philippines|Revolutionary Government of the Philippines]] and the drafting of the Malolos Constitution by a congress of revolutionary delegates, the Philippine Republic was inaugurated at Barasoain church in Malolos on 23 January 1899, with Emilio Aguinaldo as president and Apolinario Mabini as head of the cabinet.
first-philippine-republic.r: The constitution established a parliamentary system with an assembly, separation of church and state, and civil rights. In practice the war with the [[s:united-states|United States]], which began on 4 February 1899, absorbed all efforts. The government moved from Malolos to San Fernando, Tarlac and other towns as American forces advanced, and turned to [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrilla]] warfare in late 1899.
first-philippine-republic.e: Aguinaldo was captured at Palanan in March 1901 and swore allegiance to the [[s:united-states|United States]]. Generals such as Miguel Malvar fought on until 1902. Though defeated, the republic became a foundation of Filipino national identity, and its flag and anthem were later adopted by the [[s:philippines|Philippines]].

french-cochinchina.t: The southern third of Vietnam, ruled directly by France as a colony from the 1860s, with Saigon as its capital and rice and rubber as its wealth.
french-cochinchina.o: [[e:france|France]] attacked Da Nang in 1858 and captured Saigon in 1859. By the Treaty of Saigon in 1862 Emperor Tu Duc of the [[s:nguyen-dynasty|Nguyen dynasty]] ceded three eastern provinces, and in 1867 Admiral de La Grandiere seized the three western ones, completing the colony of [[s:nguyen-lords|Cochinchina]].
french-cochinchina.r: Unlike the [[e:protectorate|protectorates]] of [[s:french-protectorate-of-annam|Annam]] and [[s:french-protectorate-of-tonkin|Tonkin]], [[s:nguyen-lords|Cochinchina]] was a full colony under French law, with an elected colonial council and a deputy in the French parliament. Canals and drainage opened the [[e:mekong-river|Mekong]] delta to [[e:rice|rice]] exports, and [[e:rubber|rubber]] plantations spread in the east. Saigon and Cholon grew into a major port with large Chinese communities. Religious movements such as Cao Dai and Hoa Hao arose.
french-cochinchina.e: After the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] [[e:france|France]] set up the [[s:autonomous-republic-of-cochinchina|Autonomous Republic of Cochinchina]] in 1946. In 1949 [[s:nguyen-lords|Cochinchina]] was merged into the [[s:state-of-vietnam|State of Vietnam]] under Bao Dai, ending its separate status.

french-ionian-islands.t: Ionian Islands under French rule after the fall of Venice, twice annexed by France between 1797 and 1814 and finally held only at Corfu.
french-ionian-islands.o: [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] destruction of the [[s:republic-of-venice|Republic of Venice]] in 1797 brought French troops to [[s:corcyra|Corfu]]. The Treaty of Campo Formio in October 1797 gave [[e:france|France]] the [[s:venetian-ionian-islands|Venetian Ionian Islands]] and their mainland outposts, which were organised as three French [[e:departement|departments]]: Corcyre, Ithaque and Mer-Egee.
french-ionian-islands.r: The French burned the Golden Book of the Venetian nobility, planted liberty trees and introduced revolutionary institutions, but their requisitions and anticlericalism alienated many islanders. A Russian-Ottoman expedition under Admiral Ushakov took the islands in 1799, creating the [[s:septinsular-republic|Septinsular Republic]]. The Treaty of Tilsit in 1807 returned them to [[e:france|France]].
french-ionian-islands.e: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] blockaded and captured most of the islands in 1809-1810, but the French governor General Donzelot held [[s:corcyra|Corfu]] until it was surrendered in 1814 after [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] abdication. The islands then became the [[s:united-states-of-the-ionian-islands|United States of the Ionian Islands]] under British protection.

free-imperial-city-of-wimpfen.t: A small imperial city on the Neckar, built beside the largest Hohenstaufen palace, that kept its freedom until 1803.
free-imperial-city-of-wimpfen.o: Wimpfen stands on a hill above the Neckar near a Roman fort. Around 1200 the Hohenstaufen built their largest imperial palace there, and the town that grew beside it received town rights. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen, Wimpfen counted as a free imperial city by about 1300, while Wimpfen im Tal below kept its collegiate church of Saint Peter.
free-imperial-city-of-wimpfen.r: A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] ran the city and its tiny territory, which lived from Neckar shipping, crafts and farming. The town adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in the 16th century, though the collegiate foundation in the valley stayed Catholic. In 1622 the Battle of Wimpfen was fought nearby, a victory for Tilly's [[e:catholic-league|Catholic League]] army over Margrave George Frederick of [[s:margraviate-of-baden-durlach|Baden-Durlach]].
free-imperial-city-of-wimpfen.e: In the mediatisation of 1802 and 1803 Wimpfen passed briefly to Baden and then to [[s:grand-duchy-of-hesse|Hesse-Darmstadt]], remaining a Hessian exclave until after the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]]. Salt springs found in 1817 made it a spa, and as Bad Wimpfen it is now part of Baden-Württemberg.

french-congo.t: France's colony north of the Congo River, founded through Brazza's treaties and notorious for its concession-company abuses.
french-congo.o: In 1880 Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed a treaty with the [[s:kingdom-of-tio|Makoko]], ruler of the Kingdom of Tio, placing land north of the [[e:congo-river|Congo River]] under French protection; [[e:brazzaville|Brazzaville]] grew from his post. The Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 recognised French claims, and the territories were united with [[s:gabon-french-colony|Gabon]] as the colony of Gabon-Congo, renamed French Congo in 1891.
french-congo.r: Brazza was commissioner-general until 1897, ruling with few resources from Libreville. From 1899 the government handed most of the land to about forty concession companies, which forced Africans to collect [[e:rubber|rubber]] and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], leading to scandals and depopulation. A commission led by Brazza investigated the abuses in 1905.
french-congo.e: In 1903 the colony was divided into [[s:gabon-french-colony|Gabon]], [[s:middle-congo|Middle Congo]] and Ubangi-Shari-[[e:chad|Chad]], and in 1910 these were organised as [[s:french-equatorial-africa|French Equatorial Africa]], with [[e:brazzaville|Brazzaville]] as capital. The concession system left a lasting legacy of depopulation and distrust.

free-imperial-city-of-metz.t: A self-governing patrician republic in Lorraine, one of the richest cities of the Empire, which France seized and held against Charles V in 1552.
free-imperial-city-of-metz.o: The citizens of Metz gradually took power from their [[e:bishop|bishops]] during the 12th century, and by the late 12th century the city governed itself under the emperor's protection, outside the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-metz|Prince-Bishopric of Metz]]. A master-échevin elected each year headed the city government from 1180.
free-imperial-city-of-metz.r: Metz was run by the paraiges, a handful of patrician family associations that monopolised offices. Its merchants and bankers lent money to princes across the region, and the city controlled a sizable rural territory. Metz fought the dukes of [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Lorraine]] and withstood a siege by Charles VII and René of [[s:county-of-anjou|Anjou]] in 1444.
free-imperial-city-of-metz.e: In 1552 Henry II of [[e:france|France]] occupied Metz under the Treaty of Chambord with German Protestant princes. [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] besieged it in the winter of 1552–1553 but Francis of Guise held it. Metz became French, which the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] confirmed in 1648.

free-state-of-thuringia.t: Union of seven small Thuringian states in 1920, which saw the first Nazi minister and later disappeared into East German districts.
free-state-of-thuringia.o: After 1918 the small Ernestine and [[s:county-of-schwarzburg|Schwarzburg]] states and Reuss sought union. On 1 May 1920 Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, Saxe-Meiningen, Saxe-Altenburg, Saxe-Gotha, [[s:principality-of-schwarzburg-rudolstadt|Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt]], [[s:principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershausen|Schwarzburg-Sondershausen]] and the [[s:peoples-state-of-reuss|People's State of Reuss]] merged into the Land of Thuringia, with Weimar as capital. Coburg chose Bavaria instead.
free-state-of-thuringia.r: Thuringia had textile, toy, glass and optical industries, including Carl Zeiss in Jena. In 1923 a left-wing government was removed by the federal army. The Bauhaus left Weimar for Dessau in 1925 under nationalist pressure. In 1930 Wilhelm Frick became Thuringia's interior minister, the first Nazi to hold a ministerial post. Buchenwald [[e:concentration-camp|concentration camp]] was built near Weimar in 1937.
free-state-of-thuringia.e: After 1945 Thuringia was in the Soviet zone and became a Land of the German Democratic Republic. In 1952 it was divided into the districts of Erfurt, Gera and Suhl; the state was re-established in 1990.

free-imperial-city-of-aachen.t: Charlemagne's favourite residence and the coronation city of German kings for six centuries, a free imperial city until the French annexed it.
free-imperial-city-of-aachen.o: [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] built his palace and the Palatine Chapel at [[e:aachen|Aachen]], around hot springs, and was buried there in 814. [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] was crowned in the chapel in 936, beginning a tradition of royal coronations. In 1166 [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]], having had Charlemagne canonised in 1165, granted the town a charter of liberties.
free-imperial-city-of-aachen.r: [[e:aachen|Aachen]] was governed by a council of patricians and [[e:guild|guild]] representatives. Some thirty German kings were crowned there until 1531. Its economy rested on cloth and brass making, as well as pilgrimage to relics shown every seven years. A great fire in 1656 destroyed much of the city, and later spas attracted European visitors.
free-imperial-city-of-aachen.e: The city hosted peace congresses in 1668 and 1748. French revolutionary troops occupied it in 1794, and it was formally annexed by [[e:france|France]] under the Treaty of Lunéville in 1801. In 1815 it became Prussian. [[e:aachen|Aachen]] Cathedral was among the first World Heritage Sites.

firdafylke.t: Petty kingdom of the western Norwegian fjords of Sunnfjord and Nordfjord, one of the realms conquered by Harald Fairhair.
firdafylke.o: Firdafylke, the land of the fjord districts between [[s:sogn|Sogn]] and Møre, is known almost entirely from Snorri Sturluson's sagas. It appears as one of the small coastal kingdoms of western [[e:norway|Norway]] in the century before unification.
firdafylke.r: Little is recorded beyond the sagas. Its people farmed the narrow fjord valleys and fished the coast, and like neighbouring fylki it had its own assembly. Many families from the district later took part in the settlement of [[s:republic-of-iceland|Iceland]].
firdafylke.e: According to Heimskringla, its king Audbjørn fell fighting Harald Fairhair at the Battle of Solskjel, and the district then passed under Harald's earls. It became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-norway|Kingdom of Norway]] and of the Gulating law province.

free-imperial-city-of-buchau.t: One of the smallest free imperial cities, a town on the Federsee that shared its island site with a powerful abbey of noblewomen.
free-imperial-city-of-buchau.o: Buchau grew on an island in the Federsee in upper Swabia beside the abbey of noble canonesses founded there in the 8th century. The townspeople gradually freed themselves from the abbess's lordship, and by 1320 the town counted as a free imperial city answerable only to the emperor.
free-imperial-city-of-buchau.r: A council governed a town of a few hundred households with almost no territory, living from fishing, farming and crafts. Relations with the [[s:imperial-abbey-of-buchau|Imperial Abbey of Buchau]] next door produced constant lawsuits. The town remained Catholic and sat on the Swabian bench of cities. From the late 16th century it was home to a notable Jewish community.
free-imperial-city-of-buchau.e: In 1803 the town was mediatised and given, together with the abbey, to the princes of [[s:principality-of-thurn-and-taxis|Thurn und Taxis]]; in 1806 it passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]]. Now Bad Buchau, it is a spa town known for the prehistoric lake settlements of the Federsee moor.

free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-hall.t: Salt-producing imperial city on the Kocher that gave its name to the heller coin and became an early stronghold of the Reformation under Johannes Brenz.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-hall.o: Hall grew around salt springs on the Kocher, worked since Celtic times. Its mint produced the Haller pfennig, or heller, from the 12th century. The town was a Hohenstaufen possession, and in 1280 King Rudolf I confirmed its independence from local lords, establishing it as an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-hall.r: Patrician families who owned shares in the salt works dominated the council until [[e:guild|guilds]] gained seats in the early 16th century. Salt boiling provided most of the city's wealth. Hall built a sizeable rural territory, buying [[s:lordship-of-limpurg|Limpurg]] castle in 1541. From 1522 the preacher Johannes Brenz led a moderate Lutheran [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] that influenced much of south-western [[e:germany|Germany]].
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-hall.e: The city was annexed by Württemberg in 1802, and the salt works became a state enterprise. It is now a town in Baden-Württemberg, its old town and the great steps of St. Michael's Church well preserved.

free-imperial-city-of-windsheim.t: Small Franconian imperial city on the Aisch, surrounded by Hohenzollern lands, which adopted the Reformation and kept its freedom until 1802.
free-imperial-city-of-windsheim.o: Windsheim grew from a Frankish royal estate and later belonged to the [[e:bishop|bishops]] of Würzburg before returning to the Empire. It was recognised as an imperial city in the mid 13th century, around 1248, on the road between [[s:free-imperial-city-of-nuremberg|Nuremberg]] and Würzburg.
free-imperial-city-of-windsheim.r: The town was governed by a council and lived from farming, wine, crafts and its market. It was surrounded by the lands of the Hohenzollern margraves of [[s:principality-of-brandenburg-ansbach|Ansbach]], on whom it depended for trade and with whom it often quarrelled. Windsheim adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 1520s and subscribed to the [[s:free-imperial-city-of-augsburg|Augsburg]] Confession soon after it was presented in 1530.
free-imperial-city-of-windsheim.e: The city lost its freedom when it was annexed by Bavaria in 1802. Its saline springs later made it a spa, renamed Bad Windsheim, and it now hosts the Franconian Open-Air Museum of rural buildings.

free-city-of-riga.t: The largest Hanseatic city of Livonia, which fought the Livonian Order and its archbishops for its liberties until it submitted to Poland in 1581.
free-city-of-riga.o: Riga was founded by [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Albert in 1201 and soon received its own town law. By the late 13th century its merchant council was strong enough to act independently, and it joined the [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]] in 1282, controlling trade along the Daugava with Polotsk and [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]].
free-city-of-riga.r: The city was governed by a council of merchants, with [[e:guild|guilds]] for merchants and craftsmen. Its rivalry with the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]] led to open war from 1297; the city even allied with pagan [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]], but the Order captured it in 1330. Riga exported [[e:fur-trade|furs]], wax, [[e:flax|flax]] and [[e:timber|timber]] and adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1522, one of the first cities outside [[e:germany|Germany]] to do so.
free-city-of-riga.e: When [[s:terra-mariana|Terra Mariana]] collapsed in 1561, Riga refused to submit and remained a free city for twenty years. In 1581 it accepted the rule of Stephen Báthory of Poland-[[e:lithuania|Lithuania]], and it later became the capital of [[s:swedish-livonia|Swedish Livonia]] and then of the [[s:governorate-of-livonia|Governorate of Livonia]].

faridkot-state.t: A Sikh princely state of the Malwa region of Punjab, ruled by Brar Jat Rajas from 1763 until 1948.
faridkot-state.o: Hamir Singh, a Brar Jat chief, established himself at Faridkot around 1763, when [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] power spread across the plains after the [[e:durrani-empire|Durrani]] wars. The town took its name from the [[e:sufism|Sufi]] saint Baba Farid.
faridkot-state.r: Faridkot came under British protection in 1809. Raja Pahar Singh sided with the British in the [[e:first-anglo-sikh-war|First Anglo-Sikh War]] in 1845 and was rewarded with land. The state had an 11-gun salute and a mostly [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] rural population; its rulers built schools, a hospital and the [[e:british-raj|Raj]] Mahal palace.
faridkot-state.e: Harinder Singh Brar acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1947 and Faridkot was merged into the [[s:patiala-and-east-punjab-states-union|Patiala and East Punjab States Union]] in 1948. His death in 1989 was followed by a long legal dispute over the family estate.

free-imperial-city-of-dortmund.t: Westphalian imperial city on the Hellweg, a leading Hanseatic town that held off Cologne in the Great Feud of 1388 to 1389.
free-imperial-city-of-dortmund.o: Dortmund grew around a royal court on the Hellweg, the trade road between the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] and the Weser. Ottonian kings held assemblies there, and by around 1220 it was the only imperial city in [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Westphalia]]. Its merchants traded across the [[e:north-sea|North Sea]] and Baltic, and it became a leading member of the [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]].
free-imperial-city-of-dortmund.r: A council of merchant patricians ruled the city. Its free court was the leading tribunal of the Vehmic courts of [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Westphalia]]. In the Great Dortmund Feud of 1388 to 1389 it withstood a siege by the Archbishop of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]] and the Count of the Mark. The city was surrounded by Mark territory and gradually lost trade. [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] was introduced in the 1560s and 1570s.
free-imperial-city-of-dortmund.e: In 1803 Dortmund lost its freedom and was given to the house of [[s:principality-of-nassau-diez|Nassau-Orange]]. It belonged to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-berg|Grand Duchy of Berg]] from 1808 and to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] from 1815, growing into a great [[e:coal|coal]] and [[e:steel|steel]] city of the Ruhr.

federated-shan-states.t: The British union of more than thirty Shan and other hereditary states of eastern Burma, created in 1922 and governed from Taunggyi.
federated-shan-states.o: In 1922 the British combined the protected Shan states and the Wa states under a federal council, separating them from ministerial [[s:myanmar|Burma]] when the Dyarchy reforms gave the province partial self-government. The commissioner was based at Taunggyi.
federated-shan-states.r: The saophas kept their hereditary positions and authority over local affairs, while a British commissioner controlled policing, finances and public works through a Federal Council of Chiefs. A common budget funded roads and schools. The federation remained separate from the parliamentary system set up in [[s:myanmar|Burma]] in 1937. Japanese and Thai forces occupied the area in the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]].
federated-shan-states.e: At the Panglong Conference of 1947 Shan leaders agreed with Aung San to join an independent [[s:myanmar|Burma]], and the Federated Shan States became Shan State of the Union of [[e:burma|Burma]] in 1948.
