first-brazilian-republic.t: Brazil's Old Republic, created by a military coup against the emperor in 1889 and dominated by the coffee and dairy oligarchies of São Paulo and Minas Gerais.
first-brazilian-republic.o: On 15 November 1889 army officers led by Marshal [[e:deodoro-da-fonseca|Deodoro da Fonseca]] overthrew Emperor [[e:pedro-ii-of-brazil|Pedro II]], a year after the abolition of [[e:slavery|slavery]] had cost the monarchy the support of planters. A federal constitution was adopted in 1891, giving the states wide autonomy and creating the Republic of the [[s:united-states|United States]] of [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]].
first-brazilian-republic.r: After the military presidencies of Deodoro and Floriano Peixoto, civilian elites took control. [[e:sao-paulo|São Paulo]] and [[s:captaincy-of-minas-gerais|Minas Gerais]] alternated the presidency in the '[[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] with milk' politics, sustained by local bosses called coronéis and limited suffrage. Coffee exports and European immigration boomed. The state crushed the religious community of Canudos in 1897. In the 1920s young officers, the tenentes, rebelled against the oligarchic system.
first-brazilian-republic.e: After the 1930 election, Getúlio Vargas of [[e:rio-grande-do-sul|Rio Grande do Sul]] led the Revolution of 1930, which deposed President Washington Luís and opened the [[s:second-brazilian-republic|Second Brazilian Republic]]. Its federal structure and the power of the states left a lasting mark on Brazilian politics.

french-togoland.t: The eastern two-thirds of German Togoland, ruled by France under League and UN mandates, which became independent Togo in 1960.
french-togoland.o: After the Allied conquest of [[s:german-togoland|German Togoland]] in 1914, [[e:france|France]] took the larger eastern part, including the capital Lome and the railways, in the division of 1916. The [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] confirmed it as a French mandate in 1922, and after 1946 it was a [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] trust territory.
french-togoland.r: [[e:france|France]] governed the territory separately from [[s:french-west-africa|French West Africa]], though often with shared officials, and promoted cocoa, [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]], [[e:cotton|cotton]] and later [[e:phosphate|phosphates]]. Its trust status allowed Togolese to petition the [[e:united-nations|United Nations]]. The Committee of Togolese Unity, led by Sylvanus Olympio, campaigned for independence and Ewe unity, while Nicolas Grunitzky led parties closer to France.
french-togoland.e: In 1956 [[e:france|France]] made it an autonomous republic with Grunitzky as prime minister, but UN-supervised elections in 1958 brought Olympio to power. [[e:togo|Togo]] became independent on 27 April 1960, and Olympio was assassinated in 1963.

free-imperial-city-of-selestat.t: An Alsatian imperial city and Decapolis member, famous for its humanist Latin school and the library of Beatus Rhenanus.
free-imperial-city-of-selestat.o: Sélestat grew around a Hohenstaufen palace and the priory of Sainte-Foy on the river Ill. [[e:frederick-ii|Frederick II]] made it a town in 1217, and in 1292 King Adolf of [[s:county-of-nassau|Nassau]] confirmed its liberties as an imperial city, answerable only to the emperor. In 1354 it was a founding member of the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-selestat.r: A council drawn from the [[e:guild|guilds]] ran the city, which prospered from wine, grain and river trade. In the later 15th century its [[e:latin|Latin]] school became a centre of Rhineland humanism, and the scholar Beatus Rhenanus left his books to the town in 1547; they survive as the Humanist Library. The city remained Catholic during the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]].
free-imperial-city-of-selestat.e: Swedish troops took Sélestat in the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]], and after 1648 [[e:france|France]] claimed the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]]. [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]] had its walls razed in 1673, and the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1679 confirmed French rule; Vauban later refortified it. It is now a town in the Bas-Rhin [[e:departement|department]] of France.

french-fifth-republic.t: The present French state, founded by de Gaulle in 1958 with a strong presidency, which ended the Algerian War and helped build the European Union.
french-fifth-republic.o: The Algerian crisis of 1958 brought down the [[s:french-fourth-republic|French Fourth Republic]]. [[e:charles-de-gaulle|Charles de Gaulle]] returned to power and a new constitution, approved by referendum in September 1958, created a powerful presidency alongside a parliament. De Gaulle became the first president in January 1959.
french-fifth-republic.r: [[e:charles-de-gaulle|De Gaulle]] ended the [[e:algerian-war|Algerian War]] with Algerian independence in 1962, introduced direct election of the president that year, built an independent nuclear deterrent and left NATO's integrated command in 1966. The May 1968 protests shook the regime. François Mitterrand's election in 1981 brought the left to power, and periods of cohabitation followed.
french-fifth-republic.e: [[e:france|France]] remains a secular republic at the centre of the [[e:european-union|European Union]], using the euro since 1999. A 2000 reform cut the presidential term to five years. Emmanuel Macron was elected president in 2017 and re-elected in 2022.

french-occupation-of-egypt.t: Bonaparte's three-year occupation of Egypt, a military failure that opened Egypt to Europe and launched modern Egyptology with the Rosetta Stone.
french-occupation-of-egypt.o: In 1798 the [[s:french-first-republic|French First Republic]] sent [[e:napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]] with an army to [[e:egypt|Egypt]] to threaten British trade with [[e:india|India]]. He landed at [[e:alexandria|Alexandria]] in July, defeated the [[e:mamluk|Mamluk]] beys at the Battle of the Pyramids and entered [[e:cairo|Cairo]], but Nelson destroyed his fleet at Aboukir Bay in August 1798.
french-occupation-of-egypt.r: The French governed through councils of Egyptian notables and [[e:ulama|ulama]], imposed new taxes and suppressed revolts in [[e:cairo|Cairo]] in 1798 and 1800. Bonaparte brought scholars who founded the Institut d'Égypte and compiled the Description de l'Égypte; the Rosetta Stone was found in 1799. After Bonaparte left, Kléber commanded until his assassination in 1800, then Menou.
french-occupation-of-egypt.e: British and Ottoman forces landed in 1801, and the French capitulated at [[e:cairo|Cairo]] and [[e:alexandria|Alexandria]] that year. The collapse of [[e:mamluk|Mamluk]] power paved the way for [[s:egypt-under-muhammad-ali|Egypt under Muhammad Ali]].

french-protectorate-of-cambodia.t: Cambodia under French protection for ninety years, which saved the kingdom from partition by Siam and Vietnam but subordinated its monarchy to colonial rule.
french-protectorate-of-cambodia.o: In 1863 King Norodom, weakened by Siamese overlordship and internal rivals, signed a treaty with [[e:france|France]] accepting a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]], partly to escape Siamese pressure. A convention in 1884 forced on him much tighter French control, provoking a rebellion from 1885 to 1887.
french-protectorate-of-cambodia.r: French résidents controlled finance, taxation and administration, while the king kept ritual authority. The capital was moved to Phnom Penh, which [[e:france|France]] rebuilt. [[e:rubber|Rubber]] plantations and [[e:rice|rice]] exports grew, but most Cambodians remained farmers, and Vietnamese clerks staffed much of the administration. In 1907 France obtained Battambang and Siem Reap, with [[e:angkor|Angkor]], from Siam. [[s:kingdom-of-cambodia-1953-1970|Cambodia]] became part of [[s:french-indochina|French Indochina]] in 1887.
french-protectorate-of-cambodia.e: [[e:japan|Japan's]] coup of March 1945 allowed King Norodom Sihanouk to proclaim the [[s:kingdom-of-kampuchea-1945|Kingdom of Kampuchea]], but [[e:france|France]] returned that autumn. Sihanouk's 'royal [[e:crusade|crusade]]' for independence succeeded in November 1953, creating the [[s:post-angkorian-cambodia|Kingdom of Cambodia]].

free-imperial-city-of-haguenau.t: Alsatian imperial city grown around Barbarossa's favourite palace, seat of the imperial bailiff and leading city of the Decapolis until France took it.
free-imperial-city-of-haguenau.o: Haguenau grew beside a castle of the Hohenstaufen dukes on an island in the Moder, in the great Haguenau Forest. [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] granted it a charter in 1164 and rebuilt the castle as an imperial palace where the regalia were kept. After the Hohenstaufen fell, it was established as an imperial city by around 1260.
free-imperial-city-of-haguenau.r: Haguenau was seat of the imperial bailiff of Alsace and, from 1354, the leading member of the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities. A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] ran its affairs, with trade, forestry and crafts as its economy. In the early 16th century it was a [[e:printing-press|printing]] centre. The city remained largely Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-haguenau.e: The [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] gave [[e:france|France]] rights in Alsace, and French troops burned Haguenau in 1677; the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679 confirmed French rule. It is now a town in Alsace, France.

federal-democratic-republic-of-nepal.t: Nepal's federal republic, created when the Constituent Assembly abolished the Shah monarchy in 2008.
federal-democratic-republic-of-nepal.o: After the 2006 People's Movement ended King Gyanendra's direct rule and the Maoist insurgency, a peace agreement brought the Maoists into politics. The elected Constituent Assembly declared [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]] a federal democratic republic on 28 May 2008, abolishing the Kingdom of [[e:nepal|Nepal]], and Ram Baran Yadav became the first president.
federal-democratic-republic-of-nepal.r: Governments have changed frequently, led by the Nepali Congress, the Communist Party of [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]] (UML) and the Maoist Centre; Pushpa Kamal Dahal (Prachanda) served several terms as prime minister. A devastating earthquake struck in 2015, and the same year a new constitution created seven federal provinces and a secular state. Remittances from workers abroad and tourism support the economy.
federal-democratic-republic-of-nepal.e: The republic continues. Youth-led protests in September 2025 forced the resignation of prime minister K. P. Sharma Oli, and an interim government under Sushila Karki was formed and called elections for March 2026.

free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.t: Republican Mecklenburg-Schwerin, which replaced one of Europe's most archaic constitutions with democracy and later an early Nazi government.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.o: Grand Duke Frederick Francis IV abdicated on 14 November 1918, and [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg-Schwerin]] became a free state. A constitution of 1920 created a parliamentary republic, replacing the estates-based system that had survived since 1755.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.r: The free state remained largely agricultural, with big estates and a rural labouring population, and its capital at [[s:county-of-schwerin|Schwerin]]. [[s:lordship-of-rostock|Rostock]] with its university and shipyards was the main town. Politics swung between Social Democrats and nationalists, and in 1932 the Nazis won a majority in the Landtag elections and formed one of the first Nazi-led state governments.
free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.e: In 1933 parliamentary rule ended and Friedrich Hildebrandt became Reich governor. On 1 January 1934 a Reich law merged it with the [[s:free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz|Free State of Mecklenburg-Strelitz]] into the [[s:free-state-of-mecklenburg|Free State of Mecklenburg]], with [[s:county-of-schwerin|Schwerin]] as capital.

free-imperial-city-of-ravensburg.t: Upper Swabian imperial city that was home to the Great Ravensburg Trading Company, one of the leading merchant houses of late medieval Europe.
free-imperial-city-of-ravensburg.o: Ravensburg grew below the Veitsburg, ancestral castle of the Guelph dukes, where Henry the Lion may have been born. The town passed to the Hohenstaufen with the Guelph inheritance. After their line ended it became an imperial city, recognised by Rudolf I around 1276.
free-imperial-city-of-ravensburg.r: A council of patricians and [[e:guild|guilds]] governed. From about 1380 to 1530 the Great Ravensburg Trading Company, owned by local families, traded linen, fustian and saffron across [[e:spain|Spain]], [[e:italy|Italy]] and [[s:county-of-flanders|Flanders]]. Paper mills made the town an early centre of German papermaking. After the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] it became one of the few bi-confessional imperial cities, with Catholics and Lutherans sharing offices under the parity of 1648.
free-imperial-city-of-ravensburg.e: Ravensburg lost its freedom in 1802 to Bavaria and passed to Württemberg in 1810. It is now a town in Baden-Württemberg, known for its towers and the Ravensburger games company.

farighunid-dynasty.t: Rulers of Guzgan in northern Afghanistan who patronised the Hudud al-Alam, the oldest surviving geography written in Persian.
farighunid-dynasty.o: The Farighunids were an Iranian dynasty ruling Guzgan (Juzjan), the region between Balkh and [[e:merv|Merv]], from at least the late 9th century. They acknowledged the [[s:samanid-empire|Samanid Empire]] as overlords and were among the most prominent local princes of Khurasan.
farighunid-dynasty.r: The Farighunids were known as patrons of learning. The Hudud al-Alam, an anonymous geography of the known world completed in 982, was dedicated to the Farighunid amir Abu'l-Harith Muhammad. They kept a court in Guzgan and married into the family of the Ghaznavid ruler Sabuktigin. Their capital is uncertain, often placed at Anbar or Shiburghan.
farighunid-dynasty.e: The Farighunids transferred their loyalty from the [[s:samanid-empire|Samanids]] to the [[s:ghaznavid-empire|Ghaznavid Empire]]. After the death of the last amir around 1010, Mahmud of Ghazni absorbed Guzgan into his realm.

free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.t: Small Hessian imperial city that became home to the Empire's supreme court in 1689, where the young Goethe trained and found the story of Werther.
free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.o: Wetzlar grew around a collegiate church on the Lahn and received town privileges from [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]], being treated as an imperial city from about 1180. It lay where trade roads crossed the river, and its cloth and leather trade made it prosperous in the 13th century, when work began on the large collegiate church known as the cathedral.
free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.r: A council under the emperor's protection governed the town, but heavy debts and feuds in the 14th century left it weak, and it relied on neighbouring Hesse and [[s:county-of-nassau|Nassau]]. Its fortunes revived when the [[e:imperial-chamber-court|Imperial Chamber Court]], the Reichskammergericht, moved there from [[s:free-imperial-city-of-speyer|Speyer]] in 1689 and stayed until 1806. Lawyers flocked to the town; Goethe worked at the court in 1772, and his stay inspired The Sorrows of Young Werther.
free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar.e: In 1803 Wetzlar lost its freedom and was given to Karl Theodor von Dalberg as a county. The [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] assigned it to the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]] in 1815. It is now a town in Hesse known for optics and the Leica camera.

free-imperial-city-of-rothenburg.t: Franconian imperial city above the Tauber whose medieval walls and streets survived almost intact, made famous by the legend of the Master Draught.
free-imperial-city-of-rothenburg.o: Rothenburg grew below a Hohenstaufen castle on a spur above the Tauber valley in the 12th century. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen, King Rudolf I confirmed its status as an imperial city in 1274, and it soon threw off the last rights of outside lords.
free-imperial-city-of-rothenburg.r: A patrician council ruled. Under the mayor Heinrich Toppler, who died in prison in 1408 after the city fell foul of King Rupert, the city built up one of the largest rural territories of any imperial city. It lived from farming, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and wool. Rothenburg adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in 1544. In 1631 it was taken by Tilly's imperial army, an episode remembered in the legend of the Master Draught.
free-imperial-city-of-rothenburg.e: Impoverished by war, the city stagnated, which preserved its medieval appearance. It lost its freedom to Bavaria in 1802 to 1803 and became a celebrated tourist destination; its old town was carefully restored after damage in 1945.

french-third-republic.t: France's longest-lasting regime since the Revolution, which built secular schools and a colonial empire, won the First World War and fell in 1940.
french-third-republic.o: After [[e:napoleon-iii|Napoleon III's]] capture at [[s:principality-of-sedan|Sedan]], [[e:paris|Paris]] proclaimed the Republic on 4 September 1870. Defeat by [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], the loss of [[s:imperial-territory-of-alsace-lorraine|Alsace-Lorraine]] and the crushing of the [[s:paris-commune|Paris Commune]] followed. A monarchist assembly could not agree on a king, and the constitutional laws of 1875 created a parliamentary republic almost by default.
french-third-republic.r: Strong parliaments and short-lived cabinets governed. Jules Ferry's laws made primary schooling free, compulsory and secular, and the 1905 law separated church and state. The Dreyfus Affair divided the nation. [[e:france|France]] built a large empire in [[e:africa|Africa]] and [[e:indochina|Indochina]]. It won the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]] under Georges Clemenceau at a cost of 1.4 million dead, and the Popular Front of Léon Blum introduced paid holidays in 1936.
french-third-republic.e: [[e:germany|Germany's]] invasion in May 1940 brought rapid defeat. On 10 July 1940 parliament voted full powers to Marshal Pétain, ending the Republic and creating [[s:vichy-france|Vichy France]].

french-protectorate-of-annam.t: Central Vietnam under French protection from 1883, where the Nguyen emperors kept their court at Hue but real power lay with the French résident.
french-protectorate-of-annam.o: After the French captured [[e:hanoi|Hanoi]] and the death of Emperor Tu Duc, the Harmand Treaty of 1883 and the Patenotre Treaty of 1884 forced the [[s:nguyen-dynasty|Nguyen dynasty]] to accept French protection. The central region, which Vietnamese called Trung Ky, became the [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] of [[s:protectorate-general-to-pacify-the-south|Annam]], while [[s:french-protectorate-of-tonkin|Tonkin]] was placed under separate arrangements.
french-protectorate-of-annam.r: The emperors at Hue kept their palaces, mandarins and Confucian rituals, but a French résident supérieur controlled policy, taxes and appointments. [[e:france|France]] deposed emperors who resisted, including Ham Nghi, who led the Can Vuong movement from 1885, and later Thanh Thai and Duy Tan. [[s:protectorate-general-to-pacify-the-south|Annam]] was poorer than [[s:french-cochinchina|Cochinchina]], with coastal [[e:rice|rice]] farming and highland plantations.
french-protectorate-of-annam.e: [[s:protectorate-general-to-pacify-the-south|Annam]] was part of [[s:french-indochina|French Indochina]] from 1887. In March 1945 [[e:japan|Japan]] ended French rule, and Bao Dai proclaimed the [[s:empire-of-vietnam|Empire of Vietnam]]. After his abdication to the [[e:viet-minh|Viet Minh]] in August 1945 the [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] ceased to exist.

funan.t: The earliest major state of mainland Southeast Asia known from Chinese records, a Mekong delta power whose port of Oc Eo linked Indian Ocean and China Sea trade.
funan.o: Funan is known mainly from Chinese envoys and histories from the 3rd century onward, which tell of a foreign [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]], Kaundinya, who married a local queen, Liu Ye, and founded the ruling line. Archaeology in the lower [[e:mekong-river|Mekong]], especially at the port of Oc Eo and the hill of [[e:angkor|Angkor]] Borei, shows canals and trading towns from the 1st century CE.
funan.r: Funan's wealth came from controlling the sea route across the isthmus and around the Gulf of [[s:thailand|Thailand]]: Oc Eo has yielded Roman coins, Indian [[e:bead|beads]] and Chinese mirrors. Its kings adopted [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] titles, [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] and Buddhist cults and Indian court culture, while a network of canals drained the delta for [[e:rice|rice]]. Chinese sources name rulers such as Fan Shiman, who extended its power by sea.
funan.e: In the 6th and early 7th centuries Funan was overtaken by its former [[e:vassal|vassal]] [[s:chenla|Chenla]], and Chinese records stop mentioning it after the 620s. Its Indianised kingship and religious traditions passed to the [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] states that followed, including the [[s:khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]] of [[e:angkor|Angkor]].

fukui-domain.t: The Echizen domain of a senior Tokugawa branch, whose lord Matsudaira Shungaku was a leading reformer in the last years of the shogunate.
fukui-domain.o: In 1601 [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] gave Echizen, with 680,000 koku, to his second son Yuki Hideyasu, who rebuilt the former castle of Shibata Katsuie at Kitanosho; the town was later renamed Fukui. The family took the surname Matsudaira.
fukui-domain.r: Hideyasu's son Matsudaira Tadanao was exiled in 1623 for misconduct, and the domain was cut in stages, falling to 320,000 koku and later less. In the 19th century Matsudaira Yoshinaga, known as Shungaku, employed Hashimoto Sanai and Yokoi Shonan, promoted Western learning, medicine and trade, and in 1862 became the [[e:shogun|shogunate]]'s director of political affairs, urging reform.
fukui-domain.e: Shungaku worked for a peaceful transfer of power, and his retainer Yuri Kimimasa drafted the [[e:charter-oath|Charter Oath]] of 1868. After abolition in 1871 the domain became part of Fukui Prefecture.

french-protectorate-of-laos.t: The French protectorate that united the Lao lands east of the Mekong from 1893 and created the borders of modern Laos.
french-protectorate-of-laos.o: After the Paknam incident of 1893, [[e:france|France]] forced Siam to cede the territories east of the [[e:mekong-river|Mekong]]. The French explorer and consul Auguste Pavie had already won the loyalty of the [[s:kingdom-of-luang-phrabang|Kingdom of Luang Phrabang]]. In 1899 the Lao territories were organised as a single unit under a résident supérieur at [[s:kingdom-of-vientiane|Vientiane]].
french-protectorate-of-laos.r: [[e:france|France]] ruled the kingdom of Luang Phrabang as a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] and the rest of [[e:laos|Laos]] directly, through provinces with French officials and Vietnamese clerks. Laos was a thinly populated backwater of [[s:french-indochina|French Indochina]], with taxes, [[e:corvee-labour|corvée]] labour and some [[e:tin|tin]] mining. Revolts by upland peoples such as the Hmong and Lao Theung broke out in 1901 to 1936.
french-protectorate-of-laos.e: [[e:japan|Japan]] ended French rule in 1945, and the [[s:lao-issara|Lao Issara]] declared independence. [[e:france|France]] returned in 1946, and in 1947 [[e:laos|Laos]] became a [[e:constitutional-monarchy|constitutional monarchy]], the [[s:kingdom-of-laos|Kingdom of Laos]], within the [[s:french-fourth-republic|French Union]], gaining full independence in 1953.

french-saint-croix.t: French colony on Saint Croix, briefly owned by the Knights of Malta, abandoned in the 1690s and finally sold to Denmark in 1733.
french-saint-croix.o: Saint Croix had been contested by English, [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and Spanish settlers. In 1650 forces sent by Philippe de Longvilliers de Poincy, governor of the French Antilles, expelled the Spanish and occupied the island. The next year it was included in the sale of French islands to the Knights Hospitaller, who held it until 1665.
french-saint-croix.r: The colony centred on a small settlement at Bassin, later Christiansted. Settlers grew tobacco, [[e:cotton|cotton]] and some [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] with enslaved labour, but disease and the humid climate took a heavy toll. After 1665 it was run by the French West [[e:india|India]] Company and then the crown, as a minor dependency of the larger French islands.
french-saint-croix.e: In 1695 and 1696 [[e:france|France]] withdrew the settlers to strengthen [[s:saint-domingue|Saint-Domingue]], leaving the island largely empty for decades. France sold it to the Danish West [[e:india|India]] and [[e:guinea|Guinea]] Company in 1733, after which it became the [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] centre of the [[s:danish-west-indies|Danish West Indies]], later part of the [[s:united-states-virgin-islands|United States Virgin Islands]].

free-imperial-city-of-weissenburg.t: A small Franconian imperial city on the old Roman frontier that governed itself as a free city until 1802.
free-imperial-city-of-weissenburg.o: Weissenburg lies beside the Roman fort of Biriciana on the Raetian limes. A Carolingian royal estate stood there, and [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne's]] attempted canal between the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] and [[e:danube|Danube]] basins, the Fossa [[s:province-of-carolina|Carolina]], lay nearby. The town was a royal possession of the Hohenstaufen and by the end of the 13th century counted as a free imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-weissenburg.r: A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] governed the town and its small territory. Its economy rested on crafts, traffic on the road from [[s:free-imperial-city-of-nuremberg|Nuremberg]] to [[s:free-imperial-city-of-augsburg|Augsburg]] and the stone quarries of the Franconian Jura. The city adopted the Lutheran [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] and belonged to the Franconian Circle. Above it stood the Wülzburg fortress, held by the margraves of the [[s:principality-of-brandenburg-ansbach|Principality of Brandenburg-Ansbach]], its constant rivals.
free-imperial-city-of-weissenburg.e: Weissenburg was occupied by Bavaria in 1802 and formally annexed in 1803 under the mediatisation of the imperial cities. It is now Weißenburg in [[s:duchy-of-bavaria|Bayern]], known for its Roman baths and a hoard of Roman treasure found there in 1979.

free-imperial-city-of-isny.t: An Allgäu linen town that bought its freedom in 1365 and turned Protestant while its abbey stayed Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-isny.o: Isny grew around a Benedictine abbey founded in 1096 by the counts of Veringen-Altshausen. The market beside the abbey became a town in the 13th century and passed to the Truchsesses of Waldburg, from whom it bought its freedom in 1365, becoming a free imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-isny.r: Isny's prosperity came from linen weaving and trade with [[e:italy|Italy]]. The town adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 16th century; around 1540 the reformer Paul Fagius ran a [[e:hebrew|Hebrew]] [[e:printing-press|printing]] press there with the scholar Elijah Levita. The Benedictine abbey, which gained its own imperial status in 1781, remained a Catholic enclave.
free-imperial-city-of-isny.e: In 1803 the town and abbey were given to the counts of Quadt as compensation for lost lands, and in 1806 they passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]]. Isny im Allgäu keeps much of its wall and towers.

former-qin.t: The Di-led empire of Fu Jian, which unified northern China for the first time since 316, then collapsed after its defeat at the Fei River in 383.
former-qin.o: Fu Hong, a Di chieftain of eastern Gansu, served [[s:later-zhao|Later Zhao]] and moved west when it collapsed. His son Fu Jian (the elder) took [[e:changan|Chang'an]] in 351 and proclaimed the state of [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]]. In 357 his nephew Fu Jian overthrew the tyrannical emperor Fu Sheng and took the title Heavenly King.
former-qin.r: Fu Jian and his chief minister Wang Meng built an effective Chinese-style administration, promoted Confucian learning and agriculture and treated defeated peoples generously. They conquered [[s:former-yan|Former Yan]] in 370, [[s:chouchi|Chouchi]] in 371, [[s:former-liang|Former Liang]] and Dai in 376 and the [[e:han-river|Han River]] fortress of [[e:xiangyang|Xiangyang]] in 379, uniting northern [[e:china|China]] and reaching into the [[e:tarim-basin|Tarim Basin]].
former-qin.e: Fu Jian's invasion of the south ended in rout at the Fei River in 383 against the [[s:eastern-jin|Eastern Jin]]. Former subjects rebelled, founding [[s:later-yan|Later Yan]] and [[s:later-qin|Later Qin]], and in 385 Yao Chang captured and killed Fu Jian. Remnants under Fu Deng and Fu Chong lingered until 394.

french-cilicia.t: The French military occupation of Cilicia after the First World War, whose collapse ended the hopes of returning Armenian refugees.
french-cilicia.o: Under the [[e:armistice-of-11-november-1918|Armistice]] of Mudros, British and then French forces occupied [[e:cilicia|Cilicia]] from late 1918, and in 1919 [[e:france|France]] took over full responsibility, administering it as part of the [[s:occupied-enemy-territory-administration|Occupied Enemy Territory Administration]]. Tens of thousands of Armenian survivors of the [[e:deportation|deportations]] returned with French support.
french-cilicia.r: [[e:france|France]] governed through military administrators such as Colonel Edouard Bremond, relying partly on the Armenian [[e:legion|Legion]]. The administration encouraged Armenian resettlement in Adana, Marash and Aintab, which alarmed Turkish Muslims. Nationalist resistance grew, and in January-February 1920 fighting in Marash ended with a French withdrawal and the deaths of thousands of [[e:armenians|Armenians]]. Sieges followed at Urfa and Aintab.
french-cilicia.e: By the Treaty of Ankara in October 1921 [[e:france|France]] recognised the nationalist [[s:government-of-the-grand-national-assembly|Government of the Grand National Assembly]] and withdrew from [[e:cilicia|Cilicia]] by early 1922. Most [[e:armenians|Armenians]] left with the French, many settling in [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and [[s:lebanese-republic|Lebanon]].

free-imperial-city-of-colmar.t: Alsatian wine town that was an imperial city and member of the Decapolis league until Louis XIV's France absorbed it in the 1670s.
free-imperial-city-of-colmar.o: [[e:colmar|Colmar]] grew from a Carolingian estate on the Lauch in Upper Alsace. The Hohenstaufen favoured it, and it received town rights in 1226 from [[e:frederick-ii|Frederick II]], becoming an imperial city. In 1354 it joined the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities under the imperial bailiff at [[s:free-imperial-city-of-haguenau|Haguenau]].
free-imperial-city-of-colmar.r: [[e:guild|Guilds]] and patricians shared power in the council. [[e:colmar|Colmar]] prospered from the Alsatian wine trade and crafts, and the painter Martin Schongauer worked there in the 15th century. The city adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in 1575. During the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years War]] it was held by Swedish and then French troops, and the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]] came under French protection.
free-imperial-city-of-colmar.e: French forces occupied [[e:colmar|Colmar]] in 1673, and the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679 confirmed French rule. It was German from 1871 to 1918 and again from 1940 to 1945, and is now a French town famous for its old quarter and the Isenheim Altarpiece.

free-territory.t: Nestor Makhno's anarchist zone in south-eastern Ukraine, run by peasant councils and defended by a revolutionary army in the Civil War.
free-territory.o: Nestor Makhno, an anarchist from Huliaipole, organised peasant partisans against the Austro-German occupiers and the [[s:ukrainian-state|Ukrainian State]] in 1918. As the Revolutionary Insurgent Army of [[e:ukraine|Ukraine]] grew, it controlled a large area between the [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]] and the Sea of Azov, which anarchists called the Free Territory.
free-territory.r: The movement rejected any state, organising regional congresses of peasants, workers and insurgents, free soviets and communes, while anarchist thinkers such as Volin ran its cultural work. In practice it was a military zone held by Makhno's highly mobile cavalry and machine-gun carts. The insurgents fought Germans, nationalists and Bolsheviks, and in September 1919 their victory at Peregonovka disrupted Denikin's march on [[e:moscow|Moscow]].
free-territory.e: In 1920 Makhno allied with the Red Army against Wrangel, but once the Whites were beaten the Bolsheviks turned on the insurgents in November. After months of fighting Makhno escaped to [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]] in August 1921 and died in [[e:paris|Paris]] in 1934.

federal-state-of-austria.t: Authoritarian Catholic corporate state in Austria between 1934 and the German annexation of 1938.
federal-state-of-austria.o: Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss suspended parliament in March 1933 and ruled by decree, banning the Communists and Austrian Nazis. After crushing the Social Democrats in the civil war of February 1934, he proclaimed a new constitution on 1 May 1934, creating the Federal State of [[e:austria|Austria]] based on Catholic corporatist ideas.
federal-state-of-austria.r: The regime ruled through a single party, the Fatherland Front, and corporate bodies in place of a parliament, drawing on the papal encyclical Quadragesimo Anno and on [[e:benito-mussolini|Mussolini's]] support. Dollfuss was murdered by Austrian Nazis in a failed putsch in July 1934. His successor Kurt Schuschnigg tried to preserve independence while yielding to German pressure under the 1936 July Agreement.
federal-state-of-austria.e: In March 1938 Schuschnigg called a referendum on independence, but under German threats he resigned. German troops entered [[e:austria|Austria]] on 12 March 1938, and the country was annexed to [[s:nazi-germany|Nazi Germany]] in the Anschluss.

free-imperial-city-of-nordhausen.t: Thuringian imperial city at the foot of the Harz, an early adopter of the Reformation and long famous for its grain spirits.
free-imperial-city-of-nordhausen.o: Nordhausen grew around a royal palace and a convent founded by Queen Matilda in the 10th century. In 1220 Emperor [[e:frederick-ii|Frederick II]] freed it from the convent's lordship, making it an imperial city. It allied with Erfurt and Mühlhausen in a Thuringian city league and traded within the Hanseatic network.
free-imperial-city-of-nordhausen.r: Patricians held power until a [[e:guild|guild]] uprising in 1375 brought craftsmen onto the council. The city was surrounded by the lands of the counts of Hohnstein and [[s:county-of-stolberg|Stolberg]] and relied on imperial protection and alliances. Nordhausen adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] very early, in the 1520s. Brewing and later grain spirits, the Nordhäuser Korn, were its best-known products.
free-imperial-city-of-nordhausen.e: The city lost its freedom in 1802 to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], belonged to the [[s:kingdom-of-westphalia|Kingdom of Westphalia]] from 1807 to 1813, and then returned to Prussia. It was heavily bombed in 1945, and it is now a town in Thuringia.

free-city-of-danzig-1807-1814.t: A Napoleonic city-state created at Tilsit, nominally free but in practice a French fortress on the Baltic.
free-city-of-danzig-1807-1814.o: After defeating [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] created the Free City of Danzig by the Treaty of Tilsit in 1807, taking the city and its surrounding territory from the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]]. It was placed under the joint protection of Prussia and the [[s:kingdom-of-saxony|Kingdom of Saxony]], whose king also ruled the [[s:duchy-of-warsaw|Duchy of Warsaw]].
free-city-of-danzig-1807-1814.r: The city had a senate and its own constitution, but real power lay with the French governor, General Jean Rapp, and a large garrison. [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] Continental System cut off Danzig's trade with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and ruined its merchants, while the city had to pay heavy contributions. It served as a base for the 1812 invasion of [[e:russia|Russia]].
free-city-of-danzig-1807-1814.e: In 1813 Russian and Prussian forces besieged the city for most of the year, and Rapp surrendered at the end of 1813, the garrison leaving in January 1814. The [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] returned Danzig to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1815.

free-imperial-city-of-memmingen.t: Swabian imperial city where the Twelve Articles of the German Peasants' War were drawn up in 1525, often called the first charter of human rights in Europe.
free-imperial-city-of-memmingen.o: Memmingen grew as a Guelph market town at the meeting of trade routes between the Allgäu and the [[e:danube|Danube]], passing to the Hohenstaufen. After their fall, King Rudolf I recognised it as an imperial city in 1286, granting it the law of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen|Überlingen]].
free-imperial-city-of-memmingen.r: [[e:guild|Guilds]] shared power with patricians on the council. Linen and the [[e:salt-trade|salt trade]] brought wealth. In 1525 representatives of the rebellious peasants met in Memmingen and adopted the Twelve Articles, drafted by Sebastian Lotzer and the preacher Christoph Schappeler. In 1530 the city joined the Tetrapolitan Confession and later adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]]. Wallenstein had his headquarters there in 1630.
free-imperial-city-of-memmingen.e: Memmingen lost its freedom in 1802 when Bavaria annexed it. It is now a town in Bavaria, which commemorates the Twelve Articles and the peasants' parliament of 1525 in its old [[e:guild|guild]] hall.

first-republic-of-venezuela.t: The first Spanish American colony to declare full independence, a federal republic that collapsed within a year amid earthquake and civil war.
first-republic-of-venezuela.o: After the Caracas junta of 19 April 1810 removed the captain-general of the [[s:captaincy-general-of-venezuela|Captaincy General of Venezuela]], a congress met in 1811. Urged on by Francisco de Miranda and the young Simón Bolívar of the Patriotic Society, it declared independence on 5 July 1811, the first such declaration in [[e:spanish-america|Spanish America]].
first-republic-of-venezuela.r: A federal constitution was adopted in December 1811, with an executive triumvirate including Cristóbal Mendoza. The republic abolished titles and the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]], but kept [[e:slavery|slavery]] and property qualifications for voting. Provinces such as Coro, Maracaibo and Guayana stayed royalist. On 26 March 1812 an earthquake destroyed Caracas and other patriot towns, and clergy presented it as divine punishment.
first-republic-of-venezuela.e: The royalist commander Domingo de Monteverde advanced on Caracas. Miranda, named dictator, capitulated at San Mateo in July 1812. He was handed to the Spanish by fellow officers, Bolívar among them, and died in a Cádiz prison in 1816.

free-imperial-city-of-munster.t: Small Alsatian imperial city in the Vosges valley of Saint Gregory, grown around an old abbey and remembered today for its cheese.
free-imperial-city-of-munster.o: [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Munster]] grew around the Benedictine abbey of Saint Gregory, founded in the 7th century in a Vosges valley west of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-colmar|Colmar]]. The town that formed beside the monastery won its freedom from the abbots and was recognised as an imperial city by Rudolf I in 1287. It later joined the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], the league of Alsatian imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-munster.r: The town shared authority over the valley with the abbey in a long and often bitter relationship. Its people lived from dairy farming, cheese, textiles and the valley's trade. The town and much of the valley adopted the Lutheran [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 1530s, while the abbey remained Catholic. [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Munster]] suffered heavily in the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years War]].
free-imperial-city-of-munster.e: French troops occupied the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], and the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1679 confirmed French [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]]. [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Munster]] was almost completely destroyed in the fighting of 1914 to 1915. It is now a town in Alsace famed for Munster cheese.

first-bulgarian-empire.t: Medieval Bulgarian state founded by Asparuh's Bulgars, which adopted Christianity, nurtured Slavonic literature and rivalled Byzantium for three centuries.
first-bulgarian-empire.o: [[e:bulgars|Bulgars]] under Khan Asparuh crossed the [[e:danube|Danube]] around 680 and defeated a Byzantine army. In 681 [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] recognised the new state, which joined Bulgars with the [[s:seven-slavic-tribes|Seven Slavic Tribes]] and the [[s:severians-balkan|Severi]]. Pliska became the first capital.
first-bulgarian-empire.r: Early khans ruled with a [[e:bulgars|Bulgar]] aristocracy; Krum killed the emperor [[e:nikephoros-i|Nikephoros I]] in 811 and took Serdica. Boris I accepted [[e:christianity|Christianity]] in 864, and the disciples of [[e:cyril-and-methodius|Cyril and Methodius]] developed Slavonic writing, including the Cyrillic alphabet, at Preslav and Ohrid. Under Simeon I (893–927), who took the title tsar, [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] dominated the [[e:balkans|Balkans]] and Preslav became the capital.
first-bulgarian-empire.e: Russian and Byzantine invasions in 968–971 took the east. Samuel ruled the west from Ohrid, but [[e:basil-ii|Basil II]] destroyed his army at Kleidion in 1014, and by 1018 [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] was annexed by [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]]. The [[s:second-bulgarian-empire|Second Bulgarian Empire]] revived it in 1185.

federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.t: Federation of Serbia and Montenegro formed in 1992 from the remains of Yugoslavia, dominated by Slobodan Milošević and marked by sanctions and war.
federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.o: As the [[s:socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia|Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia]] broke apart, the two remaining republics, [[s:serbia-and-montenegro|Serbia and Montenegro]], adopted a new constitution on 27 April 1992 creating the Federal Republic of [[e:yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]]. It claimed to be the continuation of the old state, a claim most other states and the [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] rejected. The writer Dobrica Ćosić was its first president.
federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.r: Real power lay with Slobodan Milošević, president of [[s:serbia|Serbia]] and from 1997 of the federation. [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] [[e:sanctions|sanctions]] over the wars in Croatia and Bosnia brought hyperinflation in 1993 and economic collapse. After the Dayton Agreement of 1995 came conflict in Kosovo, NATO bombing in 1999 and Kosovo's placement under UN administration. [[s:montenegro|Montenegro]] under Milo Đukanović increasingly went its own way.
federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.e: Milošević was overthrown in the protests of 5 October 2000 after losing the election to Vojislav Koštunica, and was later sent to The Hague. The EU-brokered [[e:belgrade|Belgrade]] Agreement of 2002 replaced the federation with [[s:serbia-and-montenegro|Serbia and Montenegro]] in February 2003.

first-austrian-republic.t: Inter-war Austrian democracy, a small state left by the Habsburg collapse that slid into civil war and dictatorship.
first-austrian-republic.o: The [[s:republic-of-german-austria|Republic of German-Austria]] was renamed the [[s:republic-of-austria|Republic of Austria]] in October 1919 after the Treaty of Saint-Germain forbade union with [[e:germany|Germany]]. The federal constitution of 1920, drafted with the help of Hans Kelsen, created a federal parliamentary republic; with Burgenland added in 1921 and [[e:vienna|Vienna]] separated from Lower [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1922, it had nine states.
first-austrian-republic.r: The republic was polarised between the Christian Social Party, strong in the countryside, and the Social Democrats of Red [[e:vienna|Vienna]], who built large council housing estates. Each side had armed militias. Chancellor Ignaz Seipel stabilised the currency with a [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] loan in 1922. The burning of the Palace of Justice in 1927 and the Depression deepened the crisis.
first-austrian-republic.e: In March 1933 Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss suspended parliament. After a brief civil war in February 1934 the Social Democrats were banned, and the May 1934 constitution created the authoritarian [[s:federal-state-of-austria|Federal State of Austria]].

french-guinea.t: The French colony on the Guinea coast and Futa Jallon highlands, which in 1958 became the only territory to reject de Gaulle's constitution and take immediate independence.
french-guinea.o: [[e:france|France]] built posts on the rivers of the [[e:guinea|Guinea]] coast from the 1860s, and in 1882 grouped them as the Rivieres du Sud, separate from [[s:french-senegal|French Senegal]]. Under Governor Noel Ballay the colony was renamed French Guinea in 1893, with its new capital at Conakry. The [[s:imamate-of-futa-jallon|Imamate of Futa Jallon]] was absorbed in 1896 and Samori Toure's lands by 1898.
french-guinea.r: French [[e:guinea|Guinea]] was part of [[s:french-west-africa|French West Africa]]. Its economy moved from wild [[e:rubber|rubber]], collected under heavy taxation, to bananas from plantations and, from the 1950s, bauxite mining. Chiefs appointed by the French collected taxes and recruited forced labour. Most people were Muslim Fulbe, Maninka and Susu, and the [[s:imamate-of-futa-jallon|Futa Jallon]] remained a centre of Islamic learning.
french-guinea.e: Ahmed Sekou Toure and his Democratic Party of [[e:guinea|Guinea]] campaigned against the 1958 constitution, and on 28 September 1958 Guinea voted no. It became independent on 2 October 1958, and [[e:france|France]] withdrew its staff and aid abruptly.

former-liang.t: The Hexi Corridor state of the Zhang family, Chinese governors loyal in name to the Jin, which kept learning and trade alive in the far north-west for decades.
former-liang.o: Zhang Gui, a Chinese official, was appointed governor of [[s:liang-liang-shidu|Liang]] province in 301 and governed from Guzang (modern Wuwei, Gansu). After the fall of the [[s:western-jin|Western Jin]] his family ruled independently; the state is conventionally dated from 320, when Zhang Mao took over after his brother's assassination.
former-liang.r: The Zhang rulers usually acknowledged the Jin emperors in the south and avoided imperial titles, governing as Chinese administrators. The [[e:gansu-corridor|Hexi Corridor]] became a refuge for scholars and refugees from the chaos to the east, and the state profited from [[e:silk-road|Silk Road]] trade. In 327 Zhang Jun set up [[s:gaochang-kingdom|Gaochang]] commandery in the Turpan basin.
former-liang.e: In 376 the [[s:former-qin|Former Qin]] ruler Fu Jian sent an army and Zhang Tianxi surrendered, taking a post at the [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] court. After the Fei River battle he fled to the [[s:eastern-jin|Eastern Jin]]. Hexi later passed to a series of [[s:liang-liang-shidu|Liang]] states, including [[s:later-liang-386-403|Later Liang]] (386-403) and [[s:northern-liang|Northern Liang]].

free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg.t: Elbe port that grew from a Carolingian fort into the Hanseatic League's second city and remains an independent city-state of Germany today.
free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg.o: [[e:hamburg|Hamburg]] began as a Carolingian fort and mission base and was refounded as a merchant settlement in the 12th century. Its port privileges are traditionally dated to a charter of [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] of 1189, actually a later forgery but still celebrated as the port's birthday. An alliance with [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck|Lübeck]] in 1241 laid foundations for the [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]].
free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg.r: Merchant families ruled through the council and the mayors, with citizens represented after the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]]. [[e:hamburg|Hamburg]] became Lutheran in 1529 under Johannes Bugenhagen's church order. Brewing, the Elbe trade and later Atlantic commerce made it rich, and the Bank of Hamburg was founded in 1619. Its imperial immediacy was confirmed in 1618, and [[e:denmark|Denmark]] accepted it in 1768.
free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg.e: Napoleonic [[e:france|France]] annexed [[e:hamburg|Hamburg]] in 1810 to 1814. It then joined the [[s:german-confederation|German Confederation]] and [[s:german-empire|German Empire]] as a city-state, survived the Great Fire of 1842, and gained Altona and other towns in 1937. It is now a federal state of [[e:germany|Germany]] and the country's largest port.

free-imperial-city-of-constance.t: Lake Constance city that hosted the great Council of 1414 to 1418, which ended the Western Schism and burned Jan Hus, before Austria absorbed it in 1548.
free-imperial-city-of-constance.o: Constance was a Roman fort and from about 600 the seat of the largest diocese in [[e:germany|Germany]]. Its citizens gradually freed themselves from the [[e:bishop|bishop]]'s rule, and the Hohenstaufen emperors granted privileges, so that by the late 12th century it was treated as an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-constance.r: Merchants and [[e:guild|guilds]] shared power in the council. The city's fine linen was sold across [[e:europe|Europe]], and it was a member of Swabian and Lake Constance city leagues. From 1414 to 1418 it hosted the Council of Constance, which elected [[e:papacy|Pope]] Martin V, ending the Western Schism, and burned Jan Hus. In the 1520s the city adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] under Ambrosius Blarer, and the [[e:bishop|bishop]] moved to Meersburg.
free-imperial-city-of-constance.e: As a member of the defeated Schmalkaldic League, Constance was taken by [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] in 1548 and given to the Austrian [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]], losing its freedom and returning to [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]]. It stayed in [[s:further-austria|Further Austria]] until passing to Baden in 1806.

french-establishments-in-oceania.t: France's scattered Pacific colony of Tahiti, the Marquesas and other island groups, which became French Polynesia after the Second World War.
french-establishments-in-oceania.o: In 1842 [[e:france|France]] annexed the Marquesas and imposed a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] on the [[s:kingdom-of-tahiti|Kingdom of Tahiti]], leading to the Franco-Tahitian War of 1844 to 1847. In 1880 Pōmare V ceded Tahiti outright, and France then annexed the Gambier Islands, the Leeward Islands, where the [[s:kingdom-of-raiatea|Kingdom of Raiatea]] resisted until 1897, and the Austral Islands by 1900.
french-establishments-in-oceania.r: A governor at Papeete ran the colony, with Catholic and Protestant missions dominant in schooling. Copra, vanilla, pearl shell and phosphate from Makatea were the main exports, and Chinese labourers came for a [[e:cotton|cotton]] plantation in the 1860s and stayed as traders. The painter Paul Gauguin made its image famous in [[e:europe|Europe]]. In 1940 the colony rallied to [[s:free-france|Free France]] and sent volunteers to the Pacific Battalion.
french-establishments-in-oceania.e: After the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]], in which the colony served as an Allied base on Bora Bora, the Establishments became an overseas territory of the [[s:french-fourth-republic|French Union]] in 1946, and Polynesians gained French citizenship. The territory was renamed [[s:french-polynesia|French Polynesia]] in 1957.

french-santo-domingo.t: French rule over the eastern, formerly Spanish part of Hispaniola, ceded in 1795, briefly held by Toussaint Louverture and ended by a Dominican revolt in 1809.
french-santo-domingo.o: In the Treaty of [[s:canton-of-basel|Basel]] of 1795 [[e:spain|Spain]] ceded its colony of Santo Domingo to [[e:france|France]]. France lacked the forces to take possession until January 1801, when [[e:toussaint-louverture|Toussaint Louverture]] marched in, unified the island and abolished [[e:slavery|slavery]]. [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] expedition under Charles Leclerc took over in 1802, and after Haitian independence French troops held on in the east.
french-santo-domingo.r: General Jean-Louis Ferrand governed from 1804, reviving trade, restoring [[e:slavery|slavery]] and encouraging raids on Haitian territory. He repulsed [[e:jean-jacques-dessalines|Jean-Jacques Dessalines]], whose army besieged Santo Domingo in 1805 and devastated [[s:spanish-jamaica|Santiago]] and Moca on its retreat. The colony was poor and depopulated, as many Spanish-speaking families had emigrated to [[e:cuba|Cuba]] and [[s:venezuela|Venezuela]].
french-santo-domingo.e: When [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] invaded [[e:spain|Spain]] in 1808, Dominican [[e:criollo-people|creoles]] led by Juan Sánchez Ramírez rose in revolt and defeated Ferrand at Palo Hincado in November 1808; Ferrand took his own life. With British naval help the rebels besieged Santo Domingo, which surrendered in July 1809, restoring Spanish rule in the period called [[s:espana-boba|España Boba]].

french-cameroon.t: The larger, French-ruled part of former German Kamerun, governed under League and UN mandates, which became independent Cameroon in 1960 after a bitter insurgency.
french-cameroon.o: British and French troops conquered [[s:kamerun|Kamerun]] in 1914-1916 and divided it, [[e:france|France]] taking about four-fifths of the territory. In 1922 the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] confirmed French rule as a mandate, and after 1946 it was a [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] trust territory. The capital was Yaounde.
french-cameroon.r: French administration used forced labour to build railways and roads and promoted cocoa, [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] and [[e:timber|timber]] exports. In August 1940 the territory rallied to [[s:free-france|Free France]]. After 1948 the Union of the Peoples of [[e:cameroon|Cameroon]], led by Ruben Um Nyobe, demanded independence and reunification with the [[s:british-cameroons|British Cameroons]]. Banned in 1955, it waged an armed revolt that French forces suppressed brutally; Um Nyobe was killed in 1958.
french-cameroon.e: [[e:france|France]] handed power to Ahmadou Ahidjo, and [[e:cameroon|Cameroon]] became independent on 1 January 1960. In 1961 the Southern Cameroons voted to join it, forming a federal republic, while the UPC insurgency continued into the 1960s.

french-mauritania.t: France's Saharan colony between Senegal and Morocco, governed for most of its history from Saint-Louis, outside its own borders.
french-mauritania.o: From 1902 Xavier Coppolani pursued a policy of peaceful penetration, using alliances with religious leaders to bring the [[s:emirate-of-trarza|Emirate of Trarza]] and the [[s:emirate-of-brakna|Emirate of Brakna]] under French protection in 1903. After Coppolani's assassination in 1905, military campaigns, including Henri Gouraud's conquest of the [[s:emirate-of-adrar|Emirate of Adrar]] in 1909, extended control northward.
french-mauritania.r: [[e:mauritania|Mauritania]] became a civil territory and, in 1920, a colony within [[s:french-west-africa|French West Africa]], administered from Saint-Louis in [[s:french-senegal|French Senegal]]. French rule was light, relying on [[e:emir|emirs]], chiefs and religious leaders, and nomadic herding society changed slowly. Resistance in the far north continued into the 1930s, and investment was minimal.
french-mauritania.e: In 1957 to 1958 [[e:france|France]] built Nouakchott as a new capital. [[e:mauritania|Mauritania]] became an autonomous Islamic Republic in 1958 and independent on 28 November 1960 under Moktar Ould Daddah, despite Moroccan claims to its territory.

federal-league.t: A league of provinces led by José Artigas that challenged Buenos Aires with a vision of federal democracy in the River Plate region.
federal-league.o: In 1814 José Gervasio Artigas, leader of the [[s:eastern-province|Eastern Province]], drew the provinces of Entre Ríos, Corrientes, Santa Fe and Misiones, and briefly [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]], into an alliance against the centralism of Buenos Aires. Artigas took the title Protector of the Free Peoples. In 1815 the Congress of Oriente met at Concepción del [[s:oriental-republic-of-uruguay|Uruguay]].
federal-league.r: The league was a loose alliance of provincial caudillos rather than a state. It defended provincial autonomy, free trade on the rivers and the rights of rural people. Artigas directed it from his camp at Purificación, near Paysandú on the [[s:oriental-republic-of-uruguay|Uruguay]] river. Indigenous Guaraní of the missions, led by Andrés Guazurary, fought with him.
federal-league.e: Portugal's invasion of the [[s:eastern-province|Banda Oriental]] from 1816 drained the league. After Artigas's defeat at Tacuarembó in 1820, his allies Francisco Ramírez and Estanislao López made peace with Buenos Aires in the Treaty of Pilar. Artigas went into exile in [[s:republic-of-paraguay|Paraguay]], where he died in 1850.

free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.t: Small Catholic imperial city surrounded by Protestant Württemberg, best known as the birthplace of the astronomer Johannes Kepler.
free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.o: Weil grew on the Würm west of Stuttgart and belonged to the Hohenstaufen, whose estates in the area passed to the Empire on their fall. It was then treated as an imperial city, confirmed in the 1270s, around 1275, its name, Weil the City, distinguishing it from nearby villages.
free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.r: A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] ruled this small town with its handful of villages. It lived from farming, crafts and markets. Surrounded entirely by the [[s:duchy-of-wurttemberg|Duchy of Württemberg]], it often quarrelled with its powerful neighbour and remained Catholic when Württemberg turned Protestant. The astronomer Johannes Kepler was born there in 1571. Much of the town was burned in 1648 near the end of the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years War]].
free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.e: Württemberg finally annexed the town in 1802, ending its long resistance to its neighbour. It is now a small town in Baden-Württemberg, with a Kepler museum in the house where the astronomer was born.

frisii.t: Germanic people of the North Sea coast who lived on artificial mounds and defied Rome by force and by diplomacy.
frisii.o: The Frisii lived on the coastal marshes of the northern [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]] between the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] and the Ems. To survive floods they built terps, artificial dwelling mounds raised over generations. They became tributaries of [[e:rome|Rome]] after the campaigns of Drusus in 12 BCE.
frisii.r: They paid tribute in ox hides. Roman sources describe no kings but war leaders and envoys; in 58 CE Verritus and Malorix travelled to [[e:rome|Rome]] and boldly took seats among the senators at [[e:pompey|Pompey's]] [[e:theatre|Theatre]], winning Nero's admiration.
frisii.e: In 28 CE they revolted against exactions, hanging tax collectors and defeating the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] at the Baduhenna wood. [[e:rome|Rome]] later abandoned control. In the 4th century rising seas left much of the coast nearly deserted, and the area was resettled, later forming the [[s:frisian-kingdom|Frisian Kingdom]].

fezzan-ghadames-military-territory.t: The Libyan Fezzan under Free French military administration after its capture by Leclerc's forces from Chad, until Libyan independence in 1951.
fezzan-ghadames-military-territory.o: In late 1942 and January 1943 [[s:free-france|Free French]] forces under Philippe Leclerc advanced from [[s:chad-french-colony|Chad (French colony)]] and took the [[s:sultanate-of-fezzan|Fezzan]] from [[s:italian-libya|Italian Libya]]. [[e:france|France]] administered it as a military territory together with the oasis of Ghadames, with Sabha as its centre.
fezzan-ghadames-military-territory.r: French officers governed in cooperation with the Sayf al-Nasr family, whose leader Ahmad Sayf al-Nasr acted as chief of the territory. Parts were administratively linked to [[s:french-algeria|French Algeria]] and southern [[e:tunisia|Tunisia]]. [[e:france|France]] hoped to keep the region to secure links between its North and Central African colonies.
fezzan-ghadames-military-territory.e: The [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] decided in 1949 that [[e:libya|Libya]] should become independent. The [[s:sultanate-of-fezzan|Fezzan]] joined the federal [[s:kingdom-of-libya|Kingdom of Libya]] at independence in December 1951 as one of its three provinces, though French troops stayed until 1956.

felsina.t: The leading Etruscan city of the Po valley, on the site of Bologna, until the Boii Gauls took it in the 4th century BCE.
felsina.o: Felsina grew from the Villanovan villages around modern [[s:republic-of-bologna|Bologna]], the area that gave the Villanovan culture its name, from the 9th century BCE. In the 6th century BCE it became a city at the centre of an Etruscan expansion north of the Apennines; Pliny called it the chief of Etruria's cities in the region.
felsina.r: Felsina controlled farmland in the Po plain and the passes over the Apennines to Etruria, and traded with the [[s:ancient-veneti|Veneti]], the Celts and the Greek port of Spina. Its cemeteries, such as the Certosa, contain the bronze Certosa situla and horseshoe-shaped stone grave stelae carved with journeys to the afterlife. Little is known of its government.
felsina.e: Celtic [[s:boii|Boii]] overran Felsina around the mid-4th century BCE, and the town became Bononia. [[e:rome|Rome]] conquered the Boii and founded the [[e:latin|Latin]] colony of Bononia in 189 BCE, from which modern [[s:republic-of-bologna|Bologna]] descends.

french-somaliland.t: France's colony on the Gulf of Aden around the port of Djibouti, the sea outlet of Ethiopia through its famous railway.
french-somaliland.o: In 1896 [[e:france|France]] combined [[s:obock|Obock]] and its [[e:protectorate|protectorates]] over the [[s:sultanate-of-tadjoura|Sultanate of Tadjoura]] and the Issa [[e:somalis|Somali]] coast into the colony of the Cote francaise des Somalis, with its capital at the new port of [[s:djibouti|Djibouti]], founded by Leonce Lagarde. The borders were fixed by agreements with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]].
french-somaliland.r: The colony lived on its port and on the [[s:djibouti|Djibouti]] to [[e:addis-ababa|Addis Ababa]] railway, completed in 1917, which carried most of [[e:ethiopia|Ethiopia's]] foreign trade. Its population of [[e:afar|Afar]] and Issa [[e:somalis|Somali]] pastoralists, Arab traders and French officials was small. During the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] it sided with Vichy until British [[e:naval-blockade|blockade]] forced it to join [[s:free-france|Free France]] in 1942.
french-somaliland.e: In referendums in 1958 and 1967 voters chose to remain French, amid protests and charges of manipulation. In 1967 the colony was renamed the [[s:french-territory-of-the-afars-and-the-issas|French Territory of the Afars and the Issas]].

free-imperial-city-of-goslar.t: Harz imperial city of the Salian emperors' palace and the Rammelsberg silver mine, whose wealth made it a leading Hanseatic town.
free-imperial-city-of-goslar.o: [[e:silver|Silver]] was found in the Rammelsberg near Goslar in the 10th century, and the Salian emperors built an imperial palace there, where Henry III often resided. The town grew rich from mining and metal trade. After the decline of royal power it gradually took control of its own affairs and was a free imperial city by around 1290.
free-imperial-city-of-goslar.r: A council dominated by mine owners and merchants ruled. [[e:silver|Silver]], [[e:copper|copper]] and lead from the Rammelsberg brought Goslar great wealth, and it joined the [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]]. The city adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in 1528. In the Treaty of Riechenberg of 1552 it lost control of the mine and forests to Henry the Younger of the [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Principality of Wolfenbüttel]], beginning a long decline.
free-imperial-city-of-goslar.e: Goslar lost its freedom in 1802 to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], belonged to the [[s:kingdom-of-westphalia|Kingdom of Westphalia]] from 1807 and to the [[s:kingdom-of-hanover|Kingdom of Hanover]] from 1816. Its old town and the Rammelsberg mine are a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.t: One of the smallest imperial cities of the Empire, a Swabian market town at the foot of the Ipf, a celebrated Celtic hillfort.
free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.o: Bopfingen lies beneath the Ipf, a hill crowned by a major Celtic princely seat of the 6th and 5th centuries BCE. The medieval town grew under the Hohenstaufen and appears among the imperial cities in the imperial tax list of 1241.
free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.r: Bopfingen was a modest market town with a tiny territory, governed by a council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] and dependent on its larger neighbour [[s:free-imperial-city-of-nordlingen|Nördlingen]] and on the Swabian city leagues. Its economy rested on farming, crafts and the local market. It adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 16th century and suffered heavily in the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years War]].
free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.e: Bopfingen lost its freedom in 1802, passing first to the [[s:electorate-of-bavaria|Electorate of Bavaria]] and in 1810 to the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]]. It is now a small town in Baden-Württemberg, and the Ipf is a protected archaeological site.

ferozepur-state.t: A Sikh chiefship on the Sutlej whose lapse to the British in 1835 gave them a forward base against the Sikh kingdom of Lahore.
ferozepur-state.o: After the fall of Mughal Sirhind in 1763 a [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] sardar took Ferozepur, an old town on the south bank of the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]].
ferozepur-state.r: Ferozepur came under British protection in 1809 as one of the Cis-[[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]] states. For much of the period it was governed by a widow of the ruling family. Little detail of its administration is recorded.
ferozepur-state.e: When the line ended in 1835 the British took Ferozepur and turned it into a cantonment facing the [[s:sikh-empire|Sikh Empire]] across the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]]. It served as the main base for the Anglo-[[e:sikhism|Sikh]] wars and remains a district town of Indian [[e:punjab|Punjab]].

free-state-of-coburg.t: Brief Franconian republic that, after a 1919 referendum, chose to join Bavaria rather than Thuringia.
free-state-of-coburg.o: Duke Charles Edward of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha abdicated in November 1918. Coburg and Gotha, legally separate since 1826, went their own ways: Gotha joined Thuringia, while Coburg became a free state of its own, with its parliament meeting in Coburg.
free-state-of-coburg.r: The free state existed only briefly and had few powers beyond managing the transition. Its main question was its future: too small to survive alone, it had to choose between the new Thuringian state and Bavaria. In a referendum on 30 November 1919, about 88 per cent of voters chose Bavaria, partly because of Coburg's Franconian ties and Bavaria's favourable terms.
free-state-of-coburg.e: Under a state treaty Coburg joined the [[s:free-state-of-bavaria|Free State of Bavaria]] on 1 July 1920, keeping certain guarantees for its institutions.

free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.t: Allgäu imperial city on the Wertach, a linen-weaving town shared by Catholics and Protestants after the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.o: Kaufbeuren grew around a royal court on the Wertach under the Guelphs and Hohenstaufen, on the road from [[s:free-imperial-city-of-augsburg|Augsburg]] into the [[e:alps|Alps]]. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen it was recognised as an imperial city by Rudolf I in 1286.
free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.r: A council of patricians and [[e:guild|guilds]] governed. Linen and fustian weaving were the main trades. The city adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]], but after 1648 Catholics and Lutherans shared its offices under the parity rules of the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]]. The Franciscan nun Crescentia of Kaufbeuren, later canonised, lived there in the 18th century.
free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.e: Kaufbeuren lost its freedom in 1802 to Bavaria. After the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] German refugees from Gablonz in [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] settled its suburb of Neugablonz, bringing their glass and jewellery industry. It remains a town in Bavaria.

fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: A line of Delta kings of largely Canaanite descent who ruled the eastern Nile Delta as the Middle Kingdom weakened.
fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: As the Thirteenth Dynasty lost its grip, around 1725 BCE a separate line of kings established itself in the eastern Delta, probably at Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a), where a large population of Levantine origin had settled. Manetho placed the dynasty at Xois in the western Delta, but most scholars now locate it at Avaris.
fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: Very little is known. The best-attested king, Nehesy, whose name means 'the Nubian', left monuments at Avaris and Tell el-Muqdam and honoured Seth as lord of Avaris. Scarabs with royal names suggest a series of short reigns. The dynasty controlled the Delta's trade with the [[e:levant|Levant]], and its population buried their dead in Canaanite fashion, with donkeys and bronze weapons.
fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: The kingdom seems to have been weakened by famine and plague, and around 1650 BCE it was replaced by the [[s:fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Hyksos]] rulers of the Fifteenth Dynasty of [[e:egypt|Egypt]], who also made Avaris their capital.

french-louisiana.t: France's colony in the Mississippi basin, founded around the Gulf coast and New Orleans, whose Creole culture still marks the state of Louisiana.
french-louisiana.o: In 1682 René-Robert Cavelier de La Salle travelled down the [[e:mississippi-river|Mississippi]] and claimed its basin for [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]], naming it [[e:louisiana|Louisiana]]. Settlement began when Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville built Fort Maurepas at Biloxi in 1699. Mobile followed in 1702, and in 1718 his brother Bienville founded New Orleans, the capital from 1722.
french-louisiana.r: John Law's Company of the Indies ran the colony from 1717 to 1731, promoting settlement in a speculative boom that collapsed in 1720. Thousands of enslaved Africans were brought, mostly from [[e:senegambia|Senegambia]], and the Code Noir of 1724 governed [[e:slavery|slavery]]. [[e:louisiana|Louisiana]] stretched in claim to the Illinois Country and depended on Native alliances, though wars with the [[s:natchez-chiefdom|Natchez chiefdom]] and the [[s:chickasaw-nation|Chickasaw Nation]] were costly. It became a crown colony in 1731.
french-louisiana.e: Facing defeat in the Seven Years War, [[e:france|France]] secretly ceded New Orleans and the land west of the [[e:mississippi-river|Mississippi]] to [[e:spain|Spain]] in 1762, creating [[s:spanish-louisiana|Spanish Louisiana]], while the eastern lands went to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1763.

free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.t: The guild-run republic on the Rhine where Gutenberg experimented with printing and Martin Bucer led the Reformation, before Louis XIV annexed it in 1681.
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.o: The [[e:burghers|burghers]] of Strasbourg had long resented the rule of their [[e:bishop|bishops]]. In 1262 they defeated Bishop Walter of [[s:county-of-hohengeroldseck|Geroldseck]] at the battle of Hausbergen and won self-government, and the city soon became a free city of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], outside the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg|Prince-Bishopric of Strasbourg]].
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.r: From 1332 the [[e:guild|guilds]] shared power with the patricians in a council and magistracy. Strasbourg traded along the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], finished its cathedral spire in 1439, and hosted [[e:johannes-gutenberg|Johannes Gutenberg's]] early work. It adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 1520s under Martin Bucer, while Jacob Sturm led its diplomacy and Johannes Sturm founded its [[e:gymnasium|Gymnasium]]. The first printed newspaper appeared there in 1605.
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.e: In 1681, during peacetime, [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV's]] troops surrounded Strasbourg and forced it to surrender. It kept its Lutheran churches and local institutions, but became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]], confirmed by the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697.

french-ivory-coast.t: The French colony on the Gulf of Guinea that became the leading coffee and cocoa producer of French West Africa and independent Ivory Coast in 1960.
french-ivory-coast.o: [[e:france|France]] signed treaties at Grand-Bassam and Assinie in 1843, and merchants such as Arthur Verdier kept a French presence. In 1887-1889 the explorer Louis-Gustave Binger secured treaties in the interior, and in 1893 the [[e:ivory-trade|Ivory]] Coast became a colony with Binger as governor. The capital moved from Grand-Bassam to Bingerville in 1900 and to Abidjan in 1934.
french-ivory-coast.r: Conquest of the forest peoples was slow and violent, culminating in Governor Gabriel Angoulvant's campaigns of 1908-1915. The colony, part of [[s:french-west-africa|French West Africa]], exported [[e:timber|timber]], [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] and cocoa, grown on European plantations and increasingly by African farmers using migrant labour from [[s:french-upper-volta|French Upper Volta]]. Forced labour favoured European planters until the African Agricultural Union of Felix Houphouet-Boigny, founded in 1944, campaigned against it; it was abolished in 1946.
french-ivory-coast.e: Houphouet-Boigny, who also served as a minister in [[e:paris|Paris]], led the territory to autonomy within the [[e:french-community|French Community]] in 1958 and to independence on 7 August 1960. He remained president until his death in 1993, and Abidjan grew into a major West African metropolis.

first-mexican-republic.t: Mexico's first federal republic, created by the Constitution of 1824 and torn by coups between liberals, conservatives and Santa Anna.
first-mexican-republic.o: After the fall of the [[s:first-mexican-empire|First Mexican Empire]], a constituent congress adopted the federal Constitution of 4 October 1824, modelled partly on the [[s:united-states|United States]] and the Spanish constitution of 1812. It created the [[s:second-federal-republic-of-mexico|United Mexican States]], with nineteen states and four territories, and Guadalupe [[s:colony-of-victoria|Victoria]], a hero of the independence war, became the first president.
first-mexican-republic.r: [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] remained the sole permitted religion, and the army and church kept their legal privileges. Politics was dominated by rival Masonic lodges and military revolts: only [[s:colony-of-victoria|Victoria]] completed his term. Vicente Guerrero abolished [[e:slavery|slavery]] in 1829, the year Santa Anna defeated a Spanish reconquest attempt at Tampico. Valentín Gómez Farías launched anticlerical reforms in 1833, and the treasury depended on customs revenue and foreign loans.
first-mexican-republic.e: Antonio López de Santa Anna turned against the reformers in 1834, and in 1835 a conservative congress replaced the federal system with centralist laws, the Siete Leyes, creating the [[s:centralist-republic-of-mexico|Centralist Republic of Mexico]]. The change helped provoke the Texas Revolution.

free-imperial-city-of-giengen.t: A small Swabian imperial city on the Brenz, later known worldwide as the home of the Steiff teddy bear.
free-imperial-city-of-giengen.o: Giengen grew on the river Brenz in eastern Swabia as a Hohenstaufen royal town. After a period in which it was pledged to the counts of [[s:county-of-helfenstein|Helfenstein]], the townspeople secured their freedom, and by 1391 Giengen was recognised as a free imperial city answerable only to the emperor.
free-imperial-city-of-giengen.r: A council governed the small town and its few villages. Giengen lived from crafts, linen and the market for the surrounding farms, and it adopted the Lutheran [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 16th century. Its position near the [[e:danube|Danube]] exposed it to war, and in 1634, during the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]], it was almost completely burned.
free-imperial-city-of-giengen.e: In 1802 Giengen was annexed by Württemberg, becoming part of the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]] in 1806. In 1880 Margarete Steiff founded her toy business there, and Giengen an der Brenz remains the home of the Steiff company.
